Also in 1971, [UEFA](/wiki/UEFA \"UEFA\") members voted to officially recognise women\\'s football,[[80]](#cite_note-BBC-Gregory-82) while the Football Association rescinded the ban that prohibited women from playing on association members\\' pitches in England.[[91]](#cite_note-Hist-93) The first [Asian Women\\'s Championship](/wiki/AFC_Women%27s_Asian_Cup \"AFC Women\\'s Asian Cup\") happened in [1975](/wiki/1975_AFC_Women%27s_Championship \"1975 AFC Women\\'s Championship\"), initially without the approval of the [AFC](/wiki/Asian_Football_Confederation \"Asian Football Confederation\"), but later recognised by them.[[92]](#cite_note-94)[[93]](#cite_note-95)\\n\\nWomen\\'s football still faces many struggles, but its worldwide growth[[94]](#cite_note-96) has seen major competitions being launched at both the [national](/wiki/Women%27s_football_around_the_world \"Women\\'s football around the world\") and [international](/wiki/International_competitions_in_women%27s_football \"International competitions in women\\'s football\") levels, mirroring the men\\'s competitions. The [FIFA Women\\'s World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup \"FIFA Women\\'s World Cup\") was inaugurated in 1991: [the first tournament](/wiki/1991_FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup \"1991 FIFA Women\\'s World Cup\") was held in China, featuring 12 teams from the six confederations. The World Cup has been held every four years since;[[95]](#cite_note-97) by [2019](/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup \"2019 FIFA Women\\'s World Cup\"), it had expanded to 24 national teams, and 1.12\\xa0billion viewers watched the competition.[[96]](#cite_note-forbes_2019wwc-98) [Four years later](/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup \"2023 FIFA Women\\'s World Cup\"), FIFA targeted the 32-team 2023 Women\\'s World Cup at an audience of 2\\xa0billion,[[97]](#cite_note-99) while more than 1.5\\xa0million tickets were sold, setting a Women\\'s World Cup record.[[98]](#cite_note-100)[[99]](#cite_note-101) Women\\'s football has been an Olympic event since [1996](/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_tournament \"Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Women\\'s tournament\").[[100]](#cite_note-102)\\n\\nNorth America is the dominant region in women\\'s football, with the [United States](/wiki/United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team \"United States women\\'s national soccer team\") winning the most FIFA Women\\'s World Cups[[101]](#cite_note-103) and Olympic tournaments. Europe and Asia come second and third in terms of international success,[[102]](#cite_note-104)[[103]](#cite_note-105) and the women\\'s game has been improving in South America.[[104]](#cite_note-106)\\n\\nGameplay\\n--------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/2._SNL_-_27._krog_-_Nafta_1903_0-0_%280-0%29_Roltek_Dob_-_1._pol%C4%8Das.webm/250px--2._SNL_-_27._krog_-_Nafta_1903_0-0_%280-0%29_Roltek_Dob_-_1._pol%C4%8Das.webm.jpg)](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ec/2._SNL_-_27._krog_-_Nafta_1903_0-0_%280-0%29_Roltek_Dob_-_1._pol%C4%8Das.webm/2._SNL_-_27._krog_-_Nafta_1903_0-0_%280-0%29_Roltek_Dob_-_1._pol%C4%8Das.webm.480p.vp9.webm)\\n\\nOne half of a professional football match (45 minutes) between Slovenian clubs [NK Nafta 1903](/wiki/NK_Nafta_1903 \"NK Nafta 1903\") and [NK Dob](/wiki/NK_Dob \"NK Dob\"). The score after the half is 0–0.\\n\\nAssociation football is played in accordance with a set of rules known as the [Laws of the Game](/wiki/Laws_of_the_Game_(association_football) \"Laws of the Game (association football)\"). The game is played using a spherical ball of 68–70\\xa0cm (27–28\\xa0in) circumference,[[105]](#cite_note-107) known as the *[football](/wiki/Ball_(association_football) \"Ball (association football)\")* (or *soccer ball*). Two teams of eleven players each compete to get the ball into the other team\\'s goal (between the posts and under the bar), thereby scoring a goal. There are situations where a goal can be disallowed, such as an [offside](/wiki/Offside_(association_football) \"Offside (association football)\") call or a [foul](/wiki/Fouls_and_misconduct_(association_football) \"Fouls and misconduct (association football)\") in the build-up to the goal. The team that has scored more goals at the end of the game is the winner; if both teams have scored an equal number of goals then the game is a draw. Each team is led by a [captain](/wiki/Captain_(association_football) \"Captain (association football)\") who has only one official responsibility as mandated by the Laws of the Game: to represent their team in the coin toss before kick-off or [penalty kicks](/wiki/Penalty_kick_(association_football) \"Penalty kick (association football)\").[[4]](#cite_note-laws51-52-5)\\n\\nThe primary law is that players other than [goalkeepers](/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) \"Goalkeeper (association football)\") may not deliberately handle the ball with their hands or arms during play, though they must use both their hands during a [throw-in](/wiki/Throw-in \"Throw-in\") restart. Although players usually use their feet to move the ball around, they may use any part of their body (notably, \"[heading](/wiki/Header_(association_football) \"Header (association football)\")\" with the forehead)[[106]](#cite_note-108) other than their hands or arms.[[107]](#cite_note-fouls-109) Within normal play, all players are free to play the ball in any direction and move throughout the pitch, though players may not pass to teammates who are in an offside position.[[108]](#cite_note-offsidelaw-110)\\n\\nDuring gameplay, players attempt to create goal-scoring opportunities through individual control of the ball, such as by [dribbling](/wiki/Dribbling \"Dribbling\"), passing the ball to a teammate, and by taking shots at the goal, which is guarded by the opposing goalkeeper. Opposing players may try to regain control of the ball by intercepting a pass or through [tackling](/wiki/Tackle_(football_move)#Association_football \"Tackle (football move)\") the opponent in possession of the ball; however, physical contact between opponents is restricted. Football is generally a free-flowing game, with play stopping only when the ball has left the field of play or when play is stopped by the [referee](/wiki/Referee_(association_football) \"Referee (association football)\") for an infringement of the rules. After a stoppage, play recommences with a specified restart.[[109]](#cite_note-restart-111)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Slidetackle.JPG/250px-Slidetackle.JPG)](/wiki/File:Slidetackle.JPG)\\n\\nA player executing a slide [tackle](/wiki/Tackle_(football_move) \"Tackle (football move)\") to dispossess an opponent\\n\\nAt a professional level, most matches produce only a few goals. For example, the [2022–23 season](/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Premier_League \"2022–23 Premier League\") of the English [Premier League](/wiki/Premier_League \"Premier League\") produced an average of 2.85 goals per match.[[110]](#cite_note-112) The Laws of the Game do not specify any player positions other than goalkeeper,[[111]](#cite_note-LAW301-113) but a number of [specialised roles](/wiki/Association_football_positions \"Association football positions\") have evolved.[[112]](#cite_note-114) Broadly, these include three main categories: [strikers](/wiki/Striker_(association_football) \"Striker (association football)\"), or forwards, whose main task is to score goals; [defenders](/wiki/Defender_(association_football) \"Defender (association football)\"), who specialise in preventing their opponents from scoring; and [midfielders](/wiki/Midfielder \"Midfielder\"), who dispossess the opposition and keep possession of the ball to pass it to the forwards on their team. Players in these positions are referred to as outfield players, to distinguish them from the goalkeeper.[[113]](#cite_note-115)\\n\\nThese positions are further subdivided according to the area of the field in which the player spends the most time. For example, there are central defenders and left and right midfielders. The ten outfield players may be arranged in any combination. The number of players in each position determines the style of the team\\'s play; more forwards and fewer defenders creates a more aggressive and offensive-minded game, while the reverse creates a slower, more defensive style of play. While players typically spend most of the game in a specific position, there are few restrictions on player movement, and players can switch positions at any time.[[114]](#cite_note-116) The layout of a team\\'s players is known as a *[formation](/wiki/Formation_(association_football) \"Formation (association football)\")*. Defining the team\\'s formation and tactics is usually the prerogative of the team\\'s [manager](/wiki/Manager_(association_football) \"Manager (association football)\").[[115]](#cite_note-117)\\n\\nLaws\\n----\\n\\n\"Rules of football\" redirects here. For the rules of other football games, see [Football](/wiki/Football \"Football\").\\n\\nFurther information: [Laws of the Game (association football)](/wiki/Laws_of_the_Game_(association_football) \"Laws of the Game (association football)\")\\n\\nThere are 17 laws in the official Laws of the Game, each containing a collection of stipulations and guidelines. The same laws are designed to apply to all levels of football for both sexes, although certain modifications for groups such as juniors, seniors and people with physical disabilities are permitted.[[c]](#cite_note-Variants-118) The laws are often framed in broad terms, which allow flexibility in their application depending on the nature of the game. The Laws of the Game are published by FIFA, but are maintained by the IFAB.[[116]](#cite_note-119) In addition to the seventeen laws, numerous IFAB decisions and other directives contribute to the regulation of association football.[[117]](#cite_note-120)[[118]](#cite_note-121) Within the United States, [Major League Soccer](/wiki/Major_League_Soccer \"Major League Soccer\") used a distinct ruleset during the 1990s,[[119]](#cite_note-122) and the [NFHS](/wiki/National_Federation_of_State_High_School_Associations \"National Federation of State High School Associations\") and [NCAA](/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association \"National Collegiate Athletic Association\") still use rulesets that are comparable to, but different from, the IFAB Laws.[[120]](#cite_note-123)\\n\\n### Players, equipment, and officials\\n\\nSee also: [Association football positions](/wiki/Association_football_positions \"Association football positions\"), [Formation (association football)](/wiki/Formation_(association_football) \"Formation (association football)\"), [Substitute (association football)](/wiki/Substitute_(association_football) \"Substitute (association football)\"), and [Kit (association football)](/wiki/Kit_(association_football) \"Kit (association football)\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Howard_Webb3.jpg/250px-Howard_Webb3.jpg)](/wiki/File:Howard_Webb3.jpg)\\n\\nThe [referee](/wiki/Referee_(association_football) \"Referee (association football)\") officiates in a football match\\n\\nEach team consists of a maximum of eleven players (excluding [substitutes](/wiki/Substitute_(association_football) \"Substitute (association football)\")), one of whom must be the [goalkeeper](/wiki/Goalkeeper_(football) \"Goalkeeper (football)\"). Competition rules may state a minimum number of players required to constitute a team, which is usually seven. Goalkeepers are the only players allowed to play the ball with their hands or arms, provided they do so within the [penalty area](/wiki/Penalty_area \"Penalty area\") in front of their own goal. Though there are a variety of [positions](/wiki/Association_football_positions \"Association football positions\") in which the outfield (non-goalkeeper) players are [strategically](/wiki/Sports_strategy \"Sports strategy\") placed by a coach, these positions are not defined or required by the Laws.[[111]](#cite_note-LAW301-113)\\n\\nThe basic equipment or *[kit](/wiki/Kit_(association_football) \"Kit (association football)\")* players are required to wear includes a shirt, shorts,[[d]](#cite_note-124) socks, footwear and adequate [shin guards](/wiki/Shin_guard \"Shin guard\"). Wearing an [athletic supporter](/wiki/Jockstrap \"Jockstrap\") with protective cup is recommended for male players by medical experts and professionals.[[121]](#cite_note-125)[[122]](#cite_note-126) [Headgear](/wiki/Association_football_headgear \"Association football headgear\") is not a required piece of equipment, but players may choose to wear it to protect themselves from head injury.[[123]](#cite_note-127) Players are forbidden to wear or use anything that is dangerous to themselves or another player, such as jewellery or watches. The goalkeeper must wear clothing that is easily distinguishable from that worn by the other players and the match officials.[[124]](#cite_note-128)\\n\\nA number of players may be replaced by substitutes during the course of the game. The maximum number of substitutions permitted in most competitive international and domestic league games is five in 90 minutes,[[125]](#cite_note-129) with each team being allowed one more if the game should go into extra-time; the permitted number may vary in other competitions or in [friendly matches](/wiki/Friendly_matches \"Friendly matches\"). Common reasons for a substitution include injury, tiredness, ineffectiveness, a tactical switch, or [timewasting](/wiki/Timewasting \"Timewasting\") at the end of a finely poised game. In standard adult matches, a player who has been substituted may not take further part in a match.[[126]](#cite_note-130) IFAB recommends \"that a match should not continue if there are fewer than seven players in either team\". Any decision regarding points awarded for abandoned games is left to the individual football associations.[[127]](#cite_note-131)\\n\\nA game is officiated by a [referee](/wiki/Referee_(association_football) \"Referee (association football)\"), who has \"full authority to enforce the Laws of the Game in connection with the match to which he has been appointed\" (Law 5), and whose decisions are final. The referee is assisted by two [assistant referees](/wiki/Assistant_referee_(association_football) \"Assistant referee (association football)\"). In many high-level games there is also a [fourth official](/wiki/Fourth_official \"Fourth official\") who assists the referee and may replace another official should the need arise.[[128]](#cite_note-132)\\n\\n[Goal line technology](/wiki/Goal_line_technology \"Goal line technology\") is used to measure if the whole ball has crossed the goal-line thereby determining whether a goal has been scored or not; this was brought in to prevent controversy. [Video assistant referees](/wiki/Video_assistant_referee \"Video assistant referee\") (VAR) have also been increasingly introduced in high-level matches to assist officials through video replays to correct clear and obvious mistakes. There are four types of calls that can be reviewed: mistaken identity in awarding a red or yellow card, goals and whether there was a violation during the build-up, direct red card decisions, and penalty decisions.[[129]](#cite_note-protocol-133)\\n\\n### Ball\\n\\nMain article: [Ball (association football)](/wiki/Ball_(association_football) \"Ball (association football)\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/2022-04-24_Fu%C3%9Fball%2C_M%C3%A4nner%2C_3._Liga%2C_1._FC_Magdeburg_-_FSV_Zwickau_IMG_4343_by_Stepro.jpg/250px-2022-04-24_Fu%C3%9Fball%2C_M%C3%A4nner%2C_3._Liga%2C_1._FC_Magdeburg_-_FSV_Zwickau_IMG_4343_by_Stepro.jpg)](/wiki/File:2022-04-24_Fu%C3%9Fball,_M%C3%A4nner,_3._Liga,_1._FC_Magdeburg_-_FSV_Zwickau_IMG_4343_by_Stepro.jpg)\\n\\nA typical ball\\n\\nThe ball is spherical with a circumference of between 68 and 70\\xa0cm (27 and 28\\xa0in), a weight in the range of 410 to 450\\xa0g (14 to 16\\xa0oz), and a pressure between 0.6 and 1.1 [standard atmospheres](/wiki/Atmosphere_(unit) \"Atmosphere (unit)\") (8.5 and 15.6 [pounds per square inch](/wiki/Pound_per_square_inch \"Pound per square inch\")) at sea level. In the past the ball was made up of leather panels sewn together, with a latex bladder for pressurisation, but modern balls at all levels of the game are now synthetic.[[130]](#cite_note-134)[[131]](#cite_note-135)\\n\\n### Pitch\\n\\nMain article: [Football pitch](/wiki/Football_pitch \"Football pitch\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Association_Football_field_diagram_-en.svg/250px-Association_Football_field_diagram_-en.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Association_Football_field_diagram_-en.svg)\\n\\nStandard pitch measurements\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Fotbollsm%C3%A5l_-_football_goal_-_Ystad-2025.jpg/250px-Fotbollsm%C3%A5l_-_football_goal_-_Ystad-2025.jpg)](/wiki/File:Fotbollsm%C3%A5l_-_football_goal_-_Ystad-2025.jpg)\\n\\nGoals in different sizes.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Linjeringsmaskin_-_Ystad_-_2025.jpg/250px-Linjeringsmaskin_-_Ystad_-_2025.jpg)](/wiki/File:Linjeringsmaskin_-_Ystad_-_2025.jpg)\\n\\nPreviously, the lines were chalked by hand with a simple chalk machine, nowadays a programmable robot is used that draws all the lines on its own with spray paint.\\n\\nAs the Laws were formulated in England, and were initially administered solely by the four British football associations within [IFAB](/wiki/IFAB \"IFAB\"), the standard dimensions of a football pitch were originally expressed in [imperial units](/wiki/Imperial_units \"Imperial units\"). The Laws now express dimensions with approximate [metric](/wiki/SI \"SI\") equivalents (followed by traditional units in brackets), though use of imperial units remains popular in English-speaking countries with a relatively recent history of [metrication](/wiki/Metrication \"Metrication\") (or only partial metrication), such as Britain.[[132]](#cite_note-136)\\n\\nThe length of the pitch, or field, for international adult matches is in the range of 100–110\\xa0m (110–120\\xa0yd) and the width is in the range of 64–75\\xa0m (70–80\\xa0yd). Fields for non-international matches may be 90–120\\xa0m (100–130\\xa0yd) in length and 45–90\\xa0m (50–100\\xa0yd) in width, provided the pitch does not become square. In 2008, the IFAB initially approved a fixed size of 105\\xa0m (115\\xa0yd) long and 68\\xa0m (74\\xa0yd) wide as a standard pitch dimension for international matches;[[133]](#cite_note-137) however, this decision was later put on hold and was never actually implemented.[[134]](#cite_note-138)\\n\\nThe longer boundary lines are *touchlines*, while the shorter boundaries (on which the goals are placed) are *goal lines*. A rectangular goal is positioned on each goal line, midway between the two touchlines.[[135]](#cite_note-139) The inner edges of the vertical goal posts must be 7.32\\xa0m (24\\xa0ft) apart, and the lower edge of the horizontal crossbar supported by the goal posts must be 2.44\\xa0m (8\\xa0ft) above the ground. Nets are usually placed behind the goal, but are not required by the Laws.[[136]](#cite_note-140)\\n\\nIn front of the goal is the penalty area. This area is marked by the goal line, two lines starting on the goal line 16.5\\xa0m (18\\xa0yd) from the goalposts and extending 16.5\\xa0m (18\\xa0yd) into the pitch perpendicular to the goal line, and a line joining them. This area has a number of functions, the most prominent being to mark where the goalkeeper may handle the ball and where a penalty foul by a member of the defending team becomes punishable by a penalty kick. Other markings define the position of the ball or players at [kick-offs](/wiki/Kick-off_(association_football) \"Kick-off (association football)\"), goal kicks, penalty kicks and corner kicks.[[137]](#cite_note-141)\\n\\n### Duration and tie-breaking methods\\n\\n#### 90-minute ordinary time\\n\\nA standard adult football match consists of two halves of 45 minutes each. Each half runs continuously, meaning that the clock is not stopped when the ball is out of play. There is usually a 15-minute half-time break between halves. The end of the match is known as full-time.[[138]](#cite_note-rule7.2-142) The referee is the official timekeeper for the match, and may make an allowance for time lost through substitutions, injured players requiring attention, or other stoppages. This added time is called \"additional time\" in FIFA documents,[[139]](#cite_note-143)[[140]](#cite_note-144) but is most commonly referred to as *stoppage time* or *injury time*, while *lost time* can also be used as a synonym. The duration of stoppage time is at the sole discretion of the referee. Stoppage time does not fully compensate for the time in which the ball is [out of play](/wiki/Ball_in_and_out_of_play \"Ball in and out of play\"), and a 90-minute game typically involves about an hour of \"effective playing time\".[[141]](#cite_note-145)[[142]](#cite_note-146) The referee alone signals the end of the match. In matches where a fourth official is appointed, towards the end of the half, the referee signals how many minutes of stoppage time they intend to add. The fourth official then informs the players and spectators by holding up a board showing this number. The signalled stoppage time may be further extended by the referee.[[138]](#cite_note-rule7.2-142) Added time was introduced because of an incident in 1891 during a match between [Stoke](/wiki/Stoke_City_F.C. \"Stoke City F.C.\") and [Aston Villa](/wiki/Aston_Villa \"Aston Villa\"). Trailing 1–0 with two minutes remaining, Stoke were awarded a penalty kick. Villa\\'s goalkeeper deliberately kicked the ball far out of play; by the time it was recovered, the clock had run out and the game was over, leaving Stoke unable to attempt the penalty.[[143]](#cite_note-147) The same law also states that the duration of either half is extended until a penalty kick to be taken or retaken is completed; thus, no game can end with an uncompleted penalty.[[144]](#cite_note-148)\\n\\nDue to the relatively high ambient temperatures in some regions of the planet, cooling breaks for the players were introduced.[[145]](#cite_note-149) Breaks could take place at the referee\\'s discretion after the 30th minute of each half if the [Wet Bulb Globe Temperature](/wiki/Wet_Bulb_Globe_Temperature \"Wet Bulb Globe Temperature\") exceeded 32\\xa0°C (90\\xa0°F); the breaks would last 3 minutes, with this time made up by an extended period of stoppage time at the end of the half.\\n\\n#### Tie-breaking\\n\\nMain article: [Determining the Outcome of a Match (association football)](/wiki/Determining_the_Outcome_of_a_Match_(association_football) \"Determining the Outcome of a Match (association football)\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Didier_Drogba_Manuel_Neuer_last_penalty_kick_Champions_League_Final_2012.jpg/250px-Didier_Drogba_Manuel_Neuer_last_penalty_kick_Champions_League_Final_2012.jpg)](/wiki/File:Didier_Drogba_Manuel_Neuer_last_penalty_kick_Champions_League_Final_2012.jpg)\\n\\nMost knockout competitions use a [penalty shoot-out](/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(football) \"Penalty shoot-out (football)\") to decide the winner if a match ends as a draw\\n\\nIn league competitions, games may end in a draw. In knockout competitions where a winner is required, various methods may be employed to break such a deadlock; some competitions may invoke [replays](/wiki/Replay_(sports) \"Replay (sports)\").[[146]](#cite_note-150) A game tied at the end of regulation time may go into [extra time](/wiki/Extra_time \"Extra time\"), which consists of two further 15-minute periods. If the score is still tied after extra time, some competitions allow the use of [penalty shoot-outs](/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) \"Penalty shoot-out (association football)\") (previously known in the Laws of the Game as \"kicks from the penalty mark\")[[147]](#cite_note-151) to determine which team will progress to the next stage of the tournament or be the champion. Goals scored during extra time periods count towards the final score of the game, but kicks from the penalty mark are only used to decide the team that progresses to the next part of the tournament, with goals scored in a penalty shoot-out not making up part of the final score.[[4]](#cite_note-laws51-52-5)\\n\\nIn competitions using [two-legged matches](/wiki/Two-legged_match \"Two-legged match\"), each team competes at home once, with an aggregate score from the two matches deciding which team progresses. Where aggregates are equal, the [away goals rule](/wiki/Away_goals_rule \"Away goals rule\") may be used to determine the winners, in which case the winner is the team that scored the most goals in the leg they played away from home. If the result is still equal, extra time and potentially a penalty shoot-out are required.[[4]](#cite_note-laws51-52-5)\\n\\n### Ball in and out of play\\n\\nMain article: [Ball in and out of play](/wiki/Ball_in_and_out_of_play \"Ball in and out of play\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Shunsuke1_20080622.jpg/250px-Shunsuke1_20080622.jpg)](/wiki/File:Shunsuke1_20080622.jpg)\\n\\nA player takes a free kick, while the opposition form a \"wall\" to try to block the ball\\n\\nUnder the Laws, the two basic states of play during a game are *ball in play* and *ball out of play*. From the beginning of each [playing period](/wiki/Playing_period \"Playing period\") with a kick-off until the end of the playing period, the ball is in play at all times, except when either the ball leaves the field of play, or play is stopped by the referee. When the ball becomes out of play, play is restarted by one of eight restart methods depending on how it went out of play:\\n\\n* [Kick-off](/wiki/Kick-off_(association_football) \"Kick-off (association football)\"): following a goal by the opposing team, or to begin each period of play.[[109]](#cite_note-restart-111)\\n* [Throw-in](/wiki/Throw-in \"Throw-in\"): when the ball has crossed the touchline; awarded to the opposing team to that which last touched the ball.[[148]](#cite_note-152)\\n* [Goal kick](/wiki/Goal_kick \"Goal kick\"): when the ball has wholly crossed the goal line without a goal having been scored and having last been touched by a player of the attacking team; awarded to defending team.[[149]](#cite_note-153)\\n* [Corner kick](/wiki/Corner_kick \"Corner kick\"): when the ball has wholly crossed the goal line without a goal having been scored and having last been touched by a player of the defending team; awarded to attacking team.[[150]](#cite_note-154)\\n* [Indirect free kick](/wiki/Indirect_free_kick \"Indirect free kick\"): awarded to the opposing team following \"non-penal\" fouls, certain technical infringements, or when play is stopped to caution or dismiss an opponent without a specific foul having occurred. A goal may not be scored directly (without the ball first touching another player) from an indirect free kick.[[151]](#cite_note-freekick-155)\\n* [Direct free kick](/wiki/Direct_free_kick \"Direct free kick\"): awarded to fouled team following certain listed \"penal\" fouls.[[151]](#cite_note-freekick-155) A goal may be scored directly from a direct free kick.\\n* [Penalty kick](/wiki/Penalty_kick_(association_football) \"Penalty kick (association football)\"): awarded to the fouled team following a foul usually punishable by a direct free kick but that has occurred within their opponent\\'s penalty area.[[152]](#cite_note-156)\\n* [Dropped-ball](/wiki/Dropped-ball \"Dropped-ball\"): occurs when the referee has stopped play for any other reason, such as a serious injury to a player, interference by an external party, or a ball becoming defective.[[109]](#cite_note-restart-111)\\n\\n### Misconduct\\n\\nMain article: [Foul (association football)](/wiki/Foul_(association_football) \"Foul (association football)\")\\n\\n#### On-field\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Yellow_card.svg/120px-Yellow_card.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Yellow_card.svg)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Red_card.svg/120px-Red_card.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Red_card.svg)\\n\\nPlayers are cautioned with a yellow card, and dismissed from the game with a red card. These colours were first introduced at the [1970 FIFA World Cup](/wiki/1970_FIFA_World_Cup \"1970 FIFA World Cup\") and used consistently since.\\n\\nA [foul](/wiki/Foul_(football) \"Foul (football)\") occurs when a player commits an offence listed in the Laws of the Game while the ball is in play. The offences that constitute a foul are listed in Law 12. Handling the ball deliberately, tripping an opponent, or pushing an opponent, are examples of \"penal fouls\", punishable by a [direct free kick](/wiki/Direct_free_kick \"Direct free kick\") or penalty kick depending on where the offence occurred. Other fouls are punishable by an [indirect free kick](/wiki/Indirect_free_kick \"Indirect free kick\").[[107]](#cite_note-fouls-109)\\n\\nThe referee may punish a player\\'s or substitute\\'s [misconduct](/wiki/Misconduct_(football) \"Misconduct (football)\") by a caution ([yellow card](/wiki/Penalty_card \"Penalty card\")) or dismissal ([red card](/wiki/Penalty_card \"Penalty card\")). A second yellow card in the same game leads to a red card, which results in a dismissal. A player given a yellow card is said to have been \"booked\", the referee writing the player\\'s name in their official notebook. If a player has been dismissed, no substitute can be brought on in their place and the player may not participate in further play. Misconduct may occur at any time, and while the offences that constitute misconduct are listed, the definitions are broad. In particular, the offence of \"unsporting behaviour\" may be used to deal with most events that violate the spirit of the game, even if they are not listed as specific offences. A referee can show a yellow or red card to a player, substitute, substituted player, and to non-players such as managers and support staff.[[107]](#cite_note-fouls-109)[[153]](#cite_note-157)\\n\\nRather than stopping play, the referee may allow play to continue if doing so will benefit the team against which an offence has been committed. This is known as \"playing an advantage\".[[154]](#cite_note-158) The referee may \"call back\" play and penalise the original offence if the anticipated advantage does not ensue within \"a few seconds\". Even if an offence is not penalised due to advantage being played, the offender may still be sanctioned for misconduct at the next stoppage of play.[[155]](#cite_note-159)\\n\\nThe referee\\'s decision in all on-pitch matters is considered final. The score of a match cannot be altered after the game, even if later evidence shows that decisions (including whether a goal was awarded or not) were incorrect.[[156]](#cite_note-160)\\n\\n#### Off-field\\n\\nSee also: [Foul (association football) §\\xa0Post-match](/wiki/Foul_(association_football)#Post-match \"Foul (association football)\")\\n\\nAlong with the general administration of the sport, football associations and competition organisers also enforce good conduct in wider aspects of the game, dealing with issues such as comments to the press, clubs\\' financial management, [doping](/wiki/Doping_in_sport \"Doping in sport\"), [age fraud](/wiki/Age_fraud_in_association_football \"Age fraud in association football\") and [match fixing](/wiki/Match_fixing \"Match fixing\"). Most competitions enforce mandatory suspensions for players who are sent off in a game.[[157]](#cite_note-FAsuspensions-161) Some on-field incidents, if considered very serious (such as allegations of racial abuse), may result in competitions deciding to impose heavier sanctions than those normally associated with a red card.[[e]](#cite_note-162) Some associations allow for appeals against player suspensions incurred on-field if clubs feel a referee was incorrect or unduly harsh.[[157]](#cite_note-FAsuspensions-161)\\n\\nSanctions for such infractions may be levied on individuals or on clubs as a whole. Penalties may include fines, point deductions (in league competitions) or even expulsion from competitions. For example, the [English Football League](/wiki/English_Football_League \"English Football League\") deduct 12 points from any team that enters [financial administration](/wiki/Administration_(British_football) \"Administration (British football)\").[[158]](#cite_note-163) Among other administrative sanctions are penalties against game forfeiture. Teams that forfeit a game or are forfeited against are awarded a technical loss or win.[[159]](#cite_note-164)\\n\\nGoverning bodies\\n----------------\\n\\nSee also: [Association football around the world](/wiki/Association_football_around_the_world \"Association football around the world\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/FIFA-Headquarter.jpg/250px-FIFA-Headquarter.jpg)](/wiki/File:FIFA-Headquarter.jpg)\\n\\n[Headquarters](/wiki/FIFA_headquarters \"FIFA headquarters\") of [FIFA](/wiki/FIFA \"FIFA\"), the world governing body of football\\n\\nThe recognised international governing body of football (and associated games, such as [futsal](/wiki/Futsal \"Futsal\") and [beach soccer](/wiki/Beach_soccer \"Beach soccer\"))[[c]](#cite_note-Variants-118) is [FIFA](/wiki/FIFA \"FIFA\"). The FIFA headquarters are located in [Zürich](/wiki/Z%C3%BCrich \"Zürich\"), Switzerland. Six regional confederations are associated with FIFA; these are:[[160]](#cite_note-confeds-165)\\n\\n* [Asia](/wiki/Asia \"Asia\"): [Asian Football Confederation](/wiki/Asian_Football_Confederation \"Asian Football Confederation\") (AFC)\\n* [Africa](/wiki/Africa \"Africa\"): [Confederation of African Football](/wiki/Confederation_of_African_Football \"Confederation of African Football\") (CAF)\\n* [Europe](/wiki/Europe \"Europe\"): [Union of European Football Associations](/wiki/Union_of_European_Football_Associations \"Union of European Football Associations\") (UEFA)\\n* [North](/wiki/North_America \"North America\")/[Central America](/wiki/Central_America \"Central America\") & [Caribbean](/wiki/Caribbean \"Caribbean\"): [Confederation of North, Central American and Caribbean Association Football](/wiki/Confederation_of_North,_Central_American_and_Caribbean_Association_Football \"Confederation of North, Central American and Caribbean Association Football\") (CONCACAF)\\n* [Oceania](/wiki/Oceania \"Oceania\"): [Oceania Football Confederation](/wiki/Oceania_Football_Confederation \"Oceania Football Confederation\") (OFC)\\n* [South America](/wiki/South_America \"South America\"): [Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol](/wiki/Confederaci%C3%B3n_Sudamericana_de_F%C3%BAtbol \"Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol\") (South American Football Confederation; CONMEBOL)\\n\\nNational associations (or national federations) oversee football within individual countries. These are generally synonymous with sovereign states (for example, the [Cameroonian Football Federation](/wiki/Cameroonian_Football_Federation \"Cameroonian Football Federation\") in Cameroon), but also include a smaller number of associations responsible for sub-national entities or autonomous regions (for example, the [Scottish Football Association](/wiki/Scottish_Football_Association \"Scottish Football Association\") in Scotland). 211 national associations are affiliated both with FIFA and with their respective continental confederations.[[160]](#cite_note-confeds-165) Other national associations may be members of continental confederations but otherwise [not participate in FIFA competitions](/wiki/Non-FIFA_international_football \"Non-FIFA international football\").[[161]](#cite_note-166)\\n\\nWhile FIFA is responsible for organising international competitions and enforcing most international regulations, the [Laws of the Game](/wiki/Laws_of_the_Game_(association_football) \"Laws of the Game (association football)\") are set by the [IFAB](/wiki/International_Football_Association_Board \"International Football Association Board\"), where each of the four UK associations holds one vote and FIFA collectively holds four votes.[[50]](#cite_note-FIFA-52)\\n\\nInternational competitions\\n--------------------------\\n\\nMain article: [List of association football competitions](/wiki/List_of_association_football_competitions \"List of association football competitions\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Ousmane_Demb%C3%A9l%C3%A9_World_Cup_Trophy.jpg/250px-Ousmane_Demb%C3%A9l%C3%A9_World_Cup_Trophy.jpg)](/wiki/File:Ousmane_Demb%C3%A9l%C3%A9_World_Cup_Trophy.jpg)\\n\\nThe [FIFA World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup \"FIFA World Cup\") is the largest international competition in football and the world\\'s most viewed sporting event\\n\\nInternational competitions in association football principally consist of two varieties: competitions involving representative national teams or those involving clubs based in multiple nations and national leagues. *International football*, without qualification, most often refers to the former.[[162]](#cite_note-167) In the case of international club competition, it is the country of origin of the clubs involved, not the nationalities of their players, that renders the competition international in nature.[[163]](#cite_note-168)\\n\\nThe major international competition in football and the most prestigious is the [World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup \"FIFA World Cup\"), organised by FIFA. This competition has taken place every four years since [1930](/wiki/1930_FIFA_World_Cup \"1930 FIFA World Cup\"), with the exception of the 1942 and 1946 tournaments, which were cancelled because of [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II \"World War II\"). As of 2022, over 200 national teams compete in qualifying tournaments within the scope of continental confederations for a place in the finals.[[164]](#cite_note-169) The finals tournament involved 32 national teams (expanding to 48 teams for the [2026 tournament](/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup \"2026 FIFA World Cup\")) competing over a four-week period.[[165]](#cite_note-170)[[f]](#cite_note-teams_number-171) The World Cup is the world\\'s most widely viewed and most followed sporting event, with the [2022 tournament](/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup \"2022 FIFA World Cup\") estimated to be watched by 5\\xa0billion people, more than 60% of the global population.[[166]](#cite_note-172) The [1958 World Cup](/wiki/1958_FIFA_World_Cup \"1958 FIFA World Cup\") saw the emergence of [Pelé](/wiki/Pel%C3%A9 \"Pelé\") as a global sporting star, a period that coincided with \"the explosive spread of television, which massively amplified his presence everywhere\".[[167]](#cite_note-173) The current champions are [Argentina](/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team \"Argentina national football team\"), who won their third title at the 2022 tournament in Qatar.[[168]](#cite_note-174) The [FIFA Women\\'s World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup \"FIFA Women\\'s World Cup\") has been held every four years since [1991](/wiki/1991_FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup \"1991 FIFA Women\\'s World Cup\"). Under the tournament\\'s current format that was expanded in 2023, national teams vie for 31 slots in a three-year [qualification phase](/wiki/FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup_qualification \"FIFA Women\\'s World Cup qualification\"), while the host nation\\'s team enters automatically as the 32nd slot.[[169]](#cite_note-175) The current champions are [Spain](/wiki/Spain_women%27s_national_football_team \"Spain women\\'s national football team\"), after winning their first title in the [2023 tournament](/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup \"2023 FIFA Women\\'s World Cup\").[[170]](#cite_note-176)\\n\\nThere has been a [football tournament](/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics \"Football at the Summer Olympics\") at every [Summer Olympic Games](/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games \"Summer Olympic Games\") since [1900](/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics \"1900 Summer Olympics\"), except at the [1932](/wiki/1932_Summer_Olympics \"1932 Summer Olympics\") games in [Los Angeles](/wiki/Los_Angeles \"Los Angeles\") when FIFA and the [International Olympic Committee](/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee \"International Olympic Committee\") (IOC) had disagreed over the status of amateur players.[[171]](#cite_note-177)[[172]](#cite_note-178) Before the inception of the World Cup, the Olympics (especially during the 1920s) were the most prestigious international event. Originally, the tournament was for amateurs only.[[49]](#cite_note-Wherebegan-51) As professionalism spread around the world, the gap in quality between the World Cup and the Olympics widened. The countries that benefited most were the [Soviet Bloc](/wiki/Soviet_Bloc \"Soviet Bloc\") countries of [Eastern Europe](/wiki/Eastern_Europe \"Eastern Europe\"), where top athletes were state-sponsored while retaining their status as amateurs. Between [1948](/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics \"1948 Summer Olympics\") and [1980](/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics \"1980 Summer Olympics\"), 23 out of 27 Olympic medals were won by Eastern Europe, with only [Sweden](/wiki/Sweden_men%27s_national_football_team \"Sweden men\\'s national football team\") (gold in 1948 and bronze in 1952), [Denmark](/wiki/Denmark_national_football_team \"Denmark national football team\") (bronze in 1948 and silver in 1960) and [Japan](/wiki/Japan_national_football_team \"Japan national football team\") (bronze in 1968) breaking their dominance. For the [1984 Los Angeles Games](/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics \"1984 Summer Olympics\"), the IOC allowed professional players to compete. Since [1992](/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics \"1992 Summer Olympics\"), male competitors must be under 23 years old, although since [1996](/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics \"1996 Summer Olympics\"), three players over the age of 23 have been allowed per squad.[[173]](#cite_note-179) A women\\'s tournament was added in 1996; in contrast to the men\\'s event, full international sides without age restrictions play the women\\'s Olympic tournament.[[174]](#cite_note-180)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Torres%2C_Mata_and_Ramos_Euro_2012_trophy_01.jpg/250px-Torres%2C_Mata_and_Ramos_Euro_2012_trophy_01.jpg)](/wiki/File:Torres,_Mata_and_Ramos_Euro_2012_trophy_01.jpg)\\n\\n[Spanish](/wiki/Spain_national_football_team \"Spain national football team\") footballers [Fernando Torres](/wiki/Fernando_Torres \"Fernando Torres\"), [Juan Mata](/wiki/Juan_Mata \"Juan Mata\"), and [Sergio Ramos](/wiki/Sergio_Ramos \"Sergio Ramos\") celebrating winning the [UEFA European Championship](/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship \"UEFA European Championship\") in [2012](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2012 \"UEFA Euro 2012\")\\n\\nAfter the World Cup, the most important international football competitions are the continental championships, which are organised by each continental confederation and contested between national teams. These are the [European Championship](/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship \"UEFA European Championship\") (UEFA), the [Copa América](/wiki/Copa_Am%C3%A9rica \"Copa América\") (CONMEBOL), the [Africa Cup of Nations](/wiki/Africa_Cup_of_Nations \"Africa Cup of Nations\") (CAF), the [Asian Cup](/wiki/AFC_Asian_Cup \"AFC Asian Cup\") (AFC), the [Gold Cup](/wiki/CONCACAF_Gold_Cup \"CONCACAF Gold Cup\") (CONCACAF) and the [Nations Cup](/wiki/OFC_Men%27s_Nations_Cup \"OFC Men\\'s Nations Cup\") (OFC).[[175]](#cite_note-CBC-Continentals-181) These competitions are not strictly limited to members of the continental confederations, with guest teams from other continents sometimes invited to compete.[[176]](#cite_note-182) The [FIFA Confederations Cup](/wiki/FIFA_Confederations_Cup \"FIFA Confederations Cup\") was contested by the winners of all six continental championships, the current FIFA World Cup champions, and the country which was hosting the next World Cup. This was generally regarded as a warm-up tournament for the upcoming FIFA World Cup and did not carry the same prestige as the World Cup itself.[[175]](#cite_note-CBC-Continentals-181) The tournament was discontinued following the [2017 edition](/wiki/2017_FIFA_Confederations_Cup \"2017 FIFA Confederations Cup\"), with its calendar slot replaced by an expanded [FIFA Club World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_Club_World_Cup \"FIFA Club World Cup\").[[177]](#cite_note-183) The [Finalissima](/wiki/Finalissima \"Finalissima\") was revived in 2022, and is contested between the Copa América and European Championship winners.[[178]](#cite_note-184) The [UEFA Nations League](/wiki/UEFA_Nations_League \"UEFA Nations League\") and the [CONCACAF Nations League](/wiki/CONCACAF_Nations_League \"CONCACAF Nations League\") were introduced in the late 2010s to replace international [friendlies](/wiki/Exhibition_match \"Exhibition match\") during the two-year cycle between major tournaments.[[179]](#cite_note-185)\\n\\nThe most prestigious competitions in club football are the respective continental championships, which are generally contested between national champions, for example, the [UEFA Champions League](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League \"UEFA Champions League\") in Europe and the [Copa Libertadores](/wiki/Copa_Libertadores \"Copa Libertadores\") in South America. The winners of each continental competition contest the [FIFA Intercontinental Cup](/wiki/FIFA_Intercontinental_Cup \"FIFA Intercontinental Cup\"), held annually, and the [FIFA Club World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_Club_World_Cup \"FIFA Club World Cup\"), held once every four years.[[180]](#cite_note-186)\\n\\nDomestic competitions\\n---------------------\\n\\nMain articles: [Geography of association football](/wiki/Geography_of_association_football \"Geography of association football\") and [Geography of women\\'s association football](/wiki/Geography_of_women%27s_association_football \"Geography of women\\'s association football\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Forcejeo_Real_Madrid_-_FC_Barcelona.jpg/250px-Forcejeo_Real_Madrid_-_FC_Barcelona.jpg)](/wiki/File:Forcejeo_Real_Madrid_-_FC_Barcelona.jpg)\\n\\nA 2009 Spanish [La Liga](/wiki/La_Liga \"La Liga\") match between [Real Madrid](/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF \"Real Madrid CF\") and [Barcelona](/wiki/FC_Barcelona \"FC Barcelona\"). The fixture, known as *[El Clásico](/wiki/El_Cl%C3%A1sico \"El Clásico\")*, is one of the most renowned in sport.[[181]](#cite_note-187)\\n\\nIn each country, football clubs are usually federated in associations or leagues that organise official tournaments among themselves, from which the champion of each country and the teams that will participate in international club tournaments emerge. There is no single system of competitions, and each national league organises them according to its own traditions.[[182]](#cite_note-188)\\n\\nThe governing bodies in each country operate [league systems](/wiki/League_system \"League system\") in a [domestic season](/wiki/Domestic_association_football_season \"Domestic association football season\"), normally comprising several [divisions](/wiki/Division_(sport) \"Division (sport)\"), in which the teams gain points throughout the season depending on results, usually [three points for a win](/wiki/Three_points_for_a_win \"Three points for a win\"), one for a draw and zero for a defeat. Teams are put into [tables](/wiki/Table_(information) \"Table (information)\"), placed in order according to points accrued. In the [Old World](/wiki/Old_World \"Old World\") (Africa, Asia and Europe), it is common for each team to play every other team in its league at home and away in each season, in a [round-robin tournament](/wiki/Round-robin_tournament \"Round-robin tournament\"). At the end of a season, which typically runs from August to May, the top team is declared the champion. The top few teams may be [promoted](/wiki/Promotion_and_relegation \"Promotion and relegation\") to a higher division, and one or more of the teams finishing at the bottom are [relegated](/wiki/Promotion_and_relegation \"Promotion and relegation\") to a lower division.[[183]](#cite_note-189)\\n\\nSome exceptions to this system occur in the [New World](/wiki/New_World \"New World\") (Americas) and Australia:\\n\\n* The majority of the Latin American leagues (including [Liga MX](/wiki/Liga_MX \"Liga MX\") from Mexico and [Liga Profesional de Fútbol](/wiki/Argentine_Primera_Divisi%C3%B3n \"Argentine Primera División\") from Argentina) divide football championships into two sections named [Apertura and Clausura](/wiki/Apertura_and_Clausura \"Apertura and Clausura\") (Spanish for *Opening* and *Closing*), awarding a champion for each.[[184]](#cite_note-190) After a first phase using points in a round-robin tournament, these leagues usually have a knockout phase, with a final deciding the champion of each Apertura and Clausura tournament. In some countries, such as Uruguay,[[185]](#cite_note-191) the winners of the Apertura and Clausura play each other in a play-off for the season title.\\n* The [Brazilian Série A](/wiki/Campeonato_Brasileiro_S%C3%A9rie_A \"Campeonato Brasileiro Série A\") (\"Brasileirão\") uses a single-season double round-robin format to determine the champion, similar to most European leagues, although it is played from April or May to December.[[186]](#cite_note-192) Brazilian clubs also participate in [state leagues](/wiki/State_football_leagues_in_Brazil \"State football leagues in Brazil\") from January to April, and at least one state league, the [Campeonato Carioca](/wiki/Campeonato_Carioca \"Campeonato Carioca\") in [Rio de Janeiro](/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro_(state) \"Rio de Janeiro (state)\"), had a [split season](/wiki/Split_season \"Split season\") format until 2020.[[187]](#cite_note-193) However, Brazil has never used an Apertura and Clausura system in its national tournament, instead employing various formats with play-offs until 2002.[[188]](#cite_note-194)\\n* [Major League Soccer](/wiki/Major_League_Soccer \"Major League Soccer\") in the United States and Canada uses a closed league system (without promotion and relegation) and a conference system, similar to that used in other sports leagues in both countries. In each conference, clubs play a round-robin schedule during the regular season, and those with the most points qualify for the play-offs, which conclude with a final to determine the champion.[[189]](#cite_note-195)\\n* The [A-League](/wiki/A-League_Men \"A-League Men\") in Australia also uses a closed league system. At the end of a regular season played in a round-robin format, the clubs with the most points compete in play-offs to determine the league champion.[[190]](#cite_note-196)\\n\\nThe teams finishing at the top of a country\\'s league may also be eligible to play in [international club competitions](/wiki/List_of_association_football_competitions \"List of association football competitions\") in the following season. Most countries supplement the league system with one or more \"cup\" competitions organised on a [knock-out](/wiki/Single_elimination_tournament \"Single elimination tournament\") basis. These include the [domestic cup](/wiki/Domestic_cup \"Domestic cup\"), which may be open to all eligible teams in a country\\'s league system—both professional and amateur—and is organised by the national federation.[[191]](#cite_note-197)\\n\\nSome countries\\' top divisions feature highly-paid star players; in smaller countries, lower divisions, and many women\\'s clubs, players may be part-timers with a second job, or amateurs. The top five European leagues – [Premier League](/wiki/Premier_League \"Premier League\") (England),[[192]](#cite_note-198) [Bundesliga](/wiki/Bundesliga \"Bundesliga\") (Germany), [La Liga](/wiki/La_Liga \"La Liga\") (Spain), [Serie A](/wiki/Serie_A \"Serie A\") (Italy), and [Ligue 1](/wiki/Ligue_1 \"Ligue 1\") (France) – attract most of the world\\'s best players and, during the 2006–07 season, each of these leagues had a total wage cost in excess of [€](/wiki/Euro \"Euro\")600\\xa0million.[[193]](#cite_note-199) These leagues also generated a combined €17.2\\xa0billion in revenue in the 2021–22 season from television contracts, matchday tickets, sponsorships, and other sources.[[194]](#cite_note-200) In the 2022–23 season, clubs in Europe\\'s \"[big five](/wiki/Big_Five_(association_football) \"Big Five (association football)\")\" leagues had an aggregate wage cost of €13\\xa0billion, with each league spending more than €1.8\\xa0billion in wages. In contrast, the combined revenue of these leagues was €19.6\\xa0billion.[[195]](#cite_note-201)\\n\\nVariants and casual play\\n------------------------\\n\\nSee also: [List of types of football](/wiki/List_of_types_of_football \"List of types of football\")\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Street_soccer_in_Lagos.jpg/250px-Street_soccer_in_Lagos.jpg)](/wiki/File:Street_soccer_in_Lagos.jpg)\\n\\nStreet play in \"Serbian Cyrillic alphabet\"): Омладински фудбалски клуб Грбаљ, Serbo-Croatian pronunciation: [[gr̩̂baʎ]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian \"Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian\")) is a [Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegro \"Montenegro\") professional [football](/wiki/Association_football \"Association football\") club based in the small town of [Radanovići](/wiki/Radanovi%C4%87i,_Kotor They currently compete in the [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League \"Montenegrin Second League\").\\n\\nHistory\\n-------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: History\")]\\n\\nThe first football club in Radanovići, which existed only few seasons, was founded in 1970. After many years, the club was refounded in June 1995[[1]](#cite_note-1) and in their first season the team gained promotion to the [Montenegrin Republic League](/wiki/Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946%E2%80%932006)#Montenegrin_Republic_League \"Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946–2006)\") for the 1996–97 season (third tier of the [FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia \"FR Yugoslavia\") football system). After only three seasons in the Republic League, in the summer of 1999, OFK Grbalj (*OFC Humpback*) became a member of the [FR Yugoslavia Second League](/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia \"1999–2000 Second League of FR Yugoslavia\"), which was the biggest success of the team until 2006.[[2]](#cite_note-2) OFK Grbalj spent four seasons in the Second Yugoslav League.  \\nAfter [Montenegrin independence](/wiki/Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 \"Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006\"), OFK Grbalj became a member of the [Montenegrin First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League \"Montenegrin First League\"). In the 2006–07 season, the team achieved third place, just behind two of the most successful teams in national competitions, [Zeta](/wiki/FK_Zeta \"FK Zeta\") and [Budućnost Podgorica](/wiki/FK_Budu%C4%87nost_Podgorica \"FK Budućnost Podgorica\"). Over the next two seasons, OFK Grbalj finished as a fourth-placed team. During subsequent seasons, the team didn\\'t achieve the same successes as in their first seasons in top-tier competition, but they were never relegated from the First League.  \\nOFK Grbalj holds two all-time records in the Montenegrin First League. On 29 May 2010 they defeated [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom \"FK Kom\") 11–0, which is the biggest margin of victory in the history of league. Five years later, on 23 May 2015, OFK Grbalj beat [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar \"FK Mornar\") in [Bar](/wiki/Bar,_Montenegro \"Bar, Montenegro\") 7–0, which is the biggest away victory in league.  \\nIn the 2016–17 season, OFK Grbalj had the greatest success in their history by reaching the [Montenegrin Cup final](/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Montenegrin_Cup \"2016–17 Montenegrin Cup\"). They lost game against [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"FK Sutjeska Nikšić\") 1–0.  \\nAfter 14 consecutive seasons in top-tier, OFK Grbalj finished as a last-placed team in [2019-20 Montenegrin First League](/wiki/2019-20_Montenegrin_First_League \"2019-20 Montenegrin First League\"). After the campaign full of disappointing results, team from Radanovići was relegated to [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League \"Montenegrin Second League\").\\n\\n### First League Record\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: First League Record\")]\\n\\nSee also: [Participants of Montenegrin First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League#All_time_tables \"Montenegrin First League\")\\n\\nFor the first time, OFK Grbalj played in Montenegrin First League on season [2006–07](/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_Montenegrin_First_League \"2006–07 Montenegrin First League\"). **Omladinski fudbalski klub Grbalj** ([Serbian Cyrillic](/wiki/Serbian_Cyrillic_alphabet "Serbian Cyrillic alphabet"): Омладински фудбалски клуб Грбаљ, Serbo-Croatian pronunciation: [[gr̩̂baʎ]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian "Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian")) is a [Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro") professional [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club based in the small town of [Radanovići](/wiki/Radanovi%C4%87i,_Kotor "Radanovići, Kotor"), municipality of [Kotor](/wiki/Kotor "Kotor"). They currently compete in the [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

History
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The first football club in Radanovići, which existed only few seasons, was founded in 1970. After many years, the club was refounded in June 1995[[1]](#cite_note-1) and in their first season the team gained promotion to the [Montenegrin Republic League](/wiki/Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946%E2%80%932006)#Montenegrin_Republic_League "Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946–2006)") for the 1996–97 season (third tier of the [FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia "FR Yugoslavia") football system). After only three seasons in the Republic League, in the summer of 1999, OFK Grbalj (*OFC Humpback*) became a member of the [FR Yugoslavia Second League](/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia "1999–2000 Second League of FR Yugoslavia"), which was the biggest success of the team until 2006.[[2]](#cite_note-2) OFK Grbalj spent four seasons in the Second Yugoslav League.  
After [Montenegrin independence](/wiki/Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 "Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006"), OFK Grbalj became a member of the [Montenegrin First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"). In the 2006–07 season, the team achieved third place, just behind two of the most successful teams in national competitions, [Zeta](/wiki/FK_Zeta "FK Zeta") and [Budućnost Podgorica](/wiki/FK_Budu%C4%87nost_Podgorica "FK Budućnost Podgorica"). Over the next two seasons, OFK Grbalj finished as a fourth-placed team. During subsequent seasons, the team didn't achieve the same successes as in their first seasons in top-tier competition, but they were never relegated from the First League.  
OFK Grbalj holds two all-time records in the Montenegrin First League. On 29 May 2010 they defeated [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") 11–0, which is the biggest margin of victory in the history of league. Five years later, on 23 May 2015, OFK Grbalj beat [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") in [Bar](/wiki/Bar,_Montenegro "Bar, Montenegro") 7–0, which is the biggest away victory in league.  
In the 2016–17 season, OFK Grbalj had the greatest success in their history by reaching the [Montenegrin Cup final](/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Montenegrin_Cup "2016–17 Montenegrin Cup"). They lost game against [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") 1–0.  
After 14 consecutive seasons in top-tier, OFK Grbalj finished as a last-placed team in [2019-20 Montenegrin First League](/wiki/2019-20_Montenegrin_First_League "2019-20 Montenegrin First League"). After the campaign full of disappointing results, team from Radanovići was relegated to [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

Stadium
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Stadium")]

Main article: [Stadion Donja Sutvara](/wiki/Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara")

OFK Grbalj play at [Stadion Donja Sutvara](/wiki/Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara"), near the main road between [Budva](/wiki/Budva "Budva") and [Kotor](/wiki/Kotor "Kotor"). Stadium capacity is 1,500 seats on one stand and it doesn't meet UEFA standards for European competitions. Except the main ground, there is a smaller artificial pitch at Donja Sutvara football complex.

The **Montenegrin Second League** ([Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegrin_language "Montenegrin language"): *Druga crnogorska fudbalska liga* – *Druga CFL* – *2. CFL*) referred to as the **Meridianbet 2. CFL** for sponsorship reasons,[[1]](#cite_note-1) is the second-top [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") league in [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro"). It is headed by the [Football Association of Montenegro](/wiki/Football_Association_of_Montenegro "Football Association of Montenegro"). Second Montenegrin League consists of 10 participants. The top team qualifies for the [First League of Montenegro](/wiki/First_League_of_Montenegro "First League of Montenegro"), the second and third one contest in a playoff match against the 8th and 9th team from the First League, while the bottom-placed two teams are relegated to any of the three [third-tier leagues](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League"), to be replaced by the two winners of a three-way promotion playoffs, contested by the winners of the three Third League divisions.

History
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Before independence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Before independence")]

Main article: [Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946-2006)](/wiki/Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946-2006) "Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946-2006)")

During the existence of [SFR Yugoslavia](/wiki/SFR_Yugoslavia "SFR Yugoslavia"), [FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia "FR Yugoslavia") and [Serbia and Montenegro](/wiki/Serbia_and_Montenegro "Serbia and Montenegro"), from 1947 to 2006, Montenegrin clubs played in federal leagues. Among them, as a second-tier competitions, were [Yugoslav Second League](/wiki/Yugoslav_Second_League "Yugoslav Second League") (1947–1992), [Second League of FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia "Second League of FR Yugoslavia") (1992–2001) and [Second League of Serbia and Montenegro](/wiki/Second_League_of_Serbia_and_Montenegro "Second League of Serbia and Montenegro") (2001–2006).   
Overall, 25 different Montenegrin teams played in Yugoslav Second League from 1947 to 2006. Most seasons in second-tier spent [FK Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") (30), followed by [FK Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") (27) and [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd") (24).

### After independence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: After independence")]

Following [Montenegrin independence referendum (2006)](/wiki/Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 "Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006"), [Football Association of Montenegro](/wiki/Football_Association_of_Montenegro "Football Association of Montenegro") established their own competitions – [First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"), Second League and [Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League").

#### 2006–16

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2006–16")]

On inaugural season [2006–07](/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_Montenegrin_Second_League "2006–07 Montenegrin Second League"), members of Second League became three teams from [Serbia and Montenegro Second League previous season](/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_Montenegrin_First_League "2005–06 Montenegrin First League") and nine from third-tier competition ([Montenegrin Republic League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Republic_League "Montenegrin Republic League")).  
Winner of the first season was [Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") who won the title after the hard struggle with [Ibar](/wiki/FK_Ibar "FK Ibar") and [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj"). Notable game from the season, Ibar – Lovćen (0:1), played in front od 4,000 spectators, finished with crowd disturbances. At the end of the season, Lovćen gained directly promotion to [Prva CFL](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"), while Bokelj won the [playoff](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") games against [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje"). Ibar didn't succeed to gain promotion to Prva CFL.  
[Next year](/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_Montenegrin_Second_League "2007–08 Montenegrin Second League"), the title and directly promotion to highest rank surprisingly gained [FK Jezero](/wiki/FK_Jezero "FK Jezero"), with four points more than [Čelik](/wiki/FK_%C4%8Celik_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Čelik Nikšić"). In the [First League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"), Čelik didn't succeed against their city rivals from [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") in two games which watched 17,000 spectators overall (0:0, 0:1). But, third-placed [FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje") made success in playoff games against [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") (1:0, 0:0) and made a comeback to First League.  
Second League winner for [season 2008–09](/wiki/2008%E2%80%9309_Montenegrin_Second_League "2008–09 Montenegrin Second League") was [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane"), while in the [playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") participated [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd") and [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar"). OFK Titograd lost against [FK Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić"), but Mornar made historical success with their first-ever promotion to Prva CFL after the games against [Jezero](/wiki/FK_Jezero "FK Jezero") (2:1, 0:0). During the season 2008–09, [Otrant](/wiki/FK_Otrant "FK Otrant") scored 12 goals on the match against [Ribnica](/wiki/FK_Ribnica "FK Ribnica") (12:2), which is the all-time record in Montenegrin Second League.  
Title for [2009–10 season](/wiki/2009%E2%80%9310_Montenegrin_Second_League "2009–10 Montenegrin Second League") won [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd"), who made comeback to First League after two seasons. Second-placed [OFK Bar](/wiki/OFK_Bar "OFK Bar") made a surprisingly success in [playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") against [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") after the penalties and made their first and last promotion to Prva CFL. Third-placed [Bratstvo](/wiki/FK_Bratstvo_Cijevna "FK Bratstvo Cijevna") from [Podgorica](/wiki/Podgorica "Podgorica") outskirts lost in playoffs against another team from [Bar](/wiki/Bar,_Montenegro "Bar, Montenegro") – [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") (0:1, 1:2).  
[Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") dominated on [season 2010–11](/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Montenegrin_Second_League "2010–11 Montenegrin Second League"), finishing first with 24 points more than second-placed team. After the [playoff games](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"), promotion to First League gained [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane"), too, while [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje"), which won the second-place, remained in Second League after unsuccessful playoff performances against [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić").  
[Next year](/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Montenegrin_Second_League "2011–12 Montenegrin Second League"), Second League title won [Čelik](/wiki/FK_%C4%8Celik_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Čelik Nikšić") from [Nikšić](/wiki/Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Nikšić"), with score of 80 points. Except first-ever promotion to the First League in their history, Čelik made notable success in [2011–12 Montenegrin Cup](/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Montenegrin_Cup "2011–12 Montenegrin Cup") during the same season. They became the first member of Second League which played in the finals and won the national Cup. In final game, played in [Podgorica City Stadium](/wiki/Podgorica_City_Stadium "Podgorica City Stadium"), Čelik defeated First-League side [Rudar](/wiki/FK_Rudar_Pljevlja "FK Rudar Pljevlja") – 2:1. Except that, for the first and so far last time in the history, both representatives of Second League won their games in [First League payoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"). Second-placed [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") eliminated [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") (2:1, 3:0), while third-placed [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje") won against [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić") (0:0, 1:0). So, after the season 2011–12, three teams from Second League moved to First League.  
Former elite-member [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić") won the title on [season 2012–13](/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Montenegrin_Second_League "2012–13 Montenegrin Second League") and made a comeback to Prva CFL. Second and third placed [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") and [Zabjelo](/wiki/FK_Zabjelo "FK Zabjelo") lost their games in the playoffs, so only Dečić made a promotion to highest rank. At the beginning of the season, [OFK Bar](/wiki/OFK_Bar "OFK Bar") withdraw due to financial difficulties, so the championship had 11 members.  
After the [edition 2013–14](/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_Montenegrin_Second_League "2013–14 Montenegrin Second League"), [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") and [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") became a members of Prva CFL – Bokelj as title winner and Berane after the playoff games. During that season, on game [Zabjelo](/wiki/FK_Zabjelo "FK Zabjelo") – [Zora](/wiki/FK_Zora "FK Zora") (5–0), player [Bojan Kopitović](/w/index.php?title=Bojan_Kopitovi%C4%87&action=edit&redlink=1 "Bojan Kopitović (page does not exist)") scored five goals, which is the all-time record in Montenegrin Second League.  
On [season 2014–15](/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Montenegrin_Second_League "2014–15 Montenegrin Second League"), title race between [Iskra](/wiki/FK_Iskra_Danilovgrad "FK Iskra Danilovgrad") and [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić") lasted until the end of championship. With two points more than their main opponents, Iskra finished first and made their first-ever promotion to the highest-level competition. But, Dečić gained promotion to Prva CFL too, after the playoff games against former national champions [Mogren](/wiki/FK_Mogren "FK Mogren") (2–1; 5–0).  
[Next year](/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_Montenegrin_Second_League "2015–16 Montenegrin Second League"), [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje") became a champion. They won the title race with biggest surprise of championship – [Cetinje](/wiki/FK_Cetinje "FK Cetinje"), while the third finished [Bratstvo](/wiki/FK_Bratstvo_Cijevna "FK Bratstvo Cijevna"). But, only Jedinstvo gained promotion. Performances of Cetinje and Bratstvo in playoffs were unsuccessful. That season had 11 members, because [Mogren](/wiki/FK_Mogren "FK Mogren") withdraw due to financial troubles before the start of competition.

#### 2016–

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2016–")]

On [season 2016–17](/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Montenegrin_Second_League "2016–17 Montenegrin Second League"), [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") secured a promotion to Prva CFL after seven years spent in lowest-level competitions. Team from [Podgorica](/wiki/Podgorica "Podgorica") outskirts won the first place, while [Ibar](/wiki/FK_Ibar "FK Ibar") and [Otrant](/wiki/FK_Otrant "FK Otrant") finished second and third, but without promotion.  
[Montenegrin Second League 2017–18](/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Montenegrin_Second_League "2017–18 Montenegrin Second League") finished with success of [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") who won the first place and direct place in [Prva CFL 2018–19](/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Montenegrin_First_League "2018–19 Montenegrin First League"). Third-placed [Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") gained promotion after the playoffs against First-League side [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") (1–0; 0–0), while the newcomer in Second League [FK Podgorica](/wiki/OFK_Mladost_Lje%C5%A1kopolje "OFK Mladost Lješkopolje"), who finished second, lost their playoff games. During the same season, last-placed [Čelik](/wiki/FK_%C4%8Celik_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Čelik Nikšić") made few negative-records at that time. Team which once won the Montenegrin Cup and played in [UEFA Europa League](/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") finished season with only 8 points, 2 wins, 28 losses, longest run without win (20 games) and one of highest loses in the history of Second League (*[Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") – Čelik 10–0*).  
[Next year](/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Montenegrin_Second_League "2017–18 Montenegrin Second League"), four weeks before the end of competition, [FK Podgorica](/wiki/OFK_Mladost_Lje%C5%A1kopolje "OFK Mladost Lješkopolje") secured the title and their first ever promotion to the top flight. At the same time, [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") and [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj"), as a second and third placed, participated in the playoffs for First League. As a two last placed teams, [Igalo](/wiki/FK_Igalo "FK Igalo") and [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") were relegated to [Montenegrin Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League").  
[Season 2019–20](/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Montenegrin_Second_League "2019–20 Montenegrin Second League") was interrupted after 30 weeks, due to the [coronavirus pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Montenegro "COVID-19 pandemic in Montenegro").[[2]](#cite_note-2) Therefore, [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić"), who had 10 points more than second-placed [Jezero](/wiki/FK_Jezero "FK Jezero"), gained direct promotion to Prva CFL. As Football Association of Montenegro decided, runner-up and third-placed squad at the moment of disruption (Jezero and [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj")), participated in the playoffs for Prva CFL. While FK Jezero gained promotion to Prva CFL, FK Bokelj was eliminated after the penalties against [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd").[[3]](#cite_note-3) From the other side, two worst-placed teams ([Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") and [Otrant](/wiki/FK_Otrant "FK Otrant")) were relegated. That was the first time in the history when FK Lovćen, the oldest Montenegrin club, went to the bottom-tier. Except that, team from [Cetinje](/wiki/Cetinje "Cetinje") was relegated to [Montenegrin Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League") only one year after they played in [Prva CFL](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League") and in the final game of [Montenegrin Cup](/wiki/Montenegrin_Cup "Montenegrin Cup").  
[Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") won the title on [season 2020–21](/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_Montenegrin_Second_League "2020–21 Montenegrin Second League") and secured comeback to top-tier after two consecutive seasons in Second League. Second and third placed [Arsenal](/wiki/FK_Arsenal "FK Arsenal") and [Igalo](/wiki/OFK_Igalo "OFK Igalo") didn't succeed to gain promotion via playoffs, as they were defeated against [Iskra](/wiki/FK_Iskra_Danilovgrad "FK Iskra Danilovgrad") and [OFK Petrovac](/wiki/OFK_Petrovac "OFK Petrovac"). Two last-placed teams – [Ibar](/wiki/FK_Ibar "FK Ibar") and [Drezga](/wiki/FK_Drezga "FK Drezga") were relegated to Third League, both after two consecutive seasons spent in second-tier. During the season, Mornar made one of the all-time biggest victories in the history of competition, against Drezga (10–0).

### Relegation and promotion

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Relegation and promotion")]

See also: [Montenegrin First League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") and [Montenegrin Third League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League#Promotion_playoffs "Montenegrin Third League")

At the end of every season, champion of Second League is directly promoted to [First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"), while last placed member of First League is moving to second-tier competition. Except that, second and third placed teams from Second League are participating in [First League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"). Their opponents are 8th and 9th team from the First League.  
From the other side, two last placed teams are directly relegated to [Montenegrin Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League"). At the end of the season, winners of three Third League groups are participating in playoffs for Second League promotion. Two best placed teams from playoffs are gaining promotion to Montenegrin Second League.

### Changes in league structure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Changes in league structure")]

In period 2006–2018, Montenegrin Second League consisted of 12 participants. From 2018 to 2019 season, the number of participants is reduced to 10, with 36 week-long competition.

* Number of teams:
  + 2006–07 to 2007–18: **12**
  + Since 2018–19: **10**
