#### Competitions

Main article: [Oldest football competitions](/wiki/Oldest_football_competitions "Oldest football competitions")

One of the longest running football fixtures is the [Cordner-Eggleston Cup](/wiki/Cordner-Eggleston_Cup "Cordner-Eggleston Cup"), contested between [Melbourne Grammar School](/wiki/Melbourne_Grammar_School "Melbourne Grammar School") and [Scotch College, Melbourne](/wiki/Scotch_College,_Melbourne "Scotch College, Melbourne") every year since 1858. It is believed by many to also be the first match of [Australian rules football](/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football"), although it was played under experimental rules in its first year. The first football trophy tournament was the Caledonian Challenge Cup, donated by the Royal [Caledonian](/wiki/Caledonians "Caledonians") Society of Melbourne, played in 1861 under the [Melbourne Rules](/wiki/Melbourne_Rules "Melbourne Rules").[[93]](#cite_note-93) The oldest football league is a rugby football competition, the [United Hospitals Challenge Cup](/wiki/United_Hospitals_Challenge_Cup "United Hospitals Challenge Cup") (1874), while the oldest rugby trophy is the [Yorkshire Cup](/wiki/Yorkshire_Cup_(rugby_union) "Yorkshire Cup (rugby union)"), contested since 1878. The [South Australian Football Association](/wiki/South_Australian_Football_Association "South Australian Football Association") (30 April 1877) is the oldest surviving Australian rules football competition. The oldest surviving soccer trophy is the [Youdan Cup](/wiki/Youdan_Cup "Youdan Cup") (1867) and the oldest national football competition is the English FA Cup (1871). [The Football League](/wiki/The_Football_League "The Football League") (1888) is recognised as the longest running association football league. [The first international Rugby football match](/wiki/1871_Scotland_versus_England_rugby_union_match "1871 Scotland versus England rugby union match") took place between Scotland and England on 27 March 1871 at [Raeburn Place](/wiki/Raeburn_Place "Raeburn Place"), Edinburgh. The [first international Association football match](/wiki/1872_Scotland_v_England_football_match "1872 Scotland v England football match") officially took place between sides representing England and Scotland on 30 November 1872 at [Hamilton Crescent](/wiki/Hamilton_Crescent "Hamilton Crescent"), the [West of Scotland Cricket Club](/wiki/West_of_Scotland_Cricket_Club "West of Scotland Cricket Club")'s ground in [Partick](/wiki/Partick "Partick"), Glasgow under the authority of the FA.

#### Modern balls

Main article: [Football (ball)](/wiki/Football_(ball) "Football (ball)")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Richard_Lindon_%281816-1887%29.jpg/250px-Richard_Lindon_%281816-1887%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Richard_Lindon_(1816-1887).jpg)

[Richard Lindon](/wiki/Richard_Lindon "Richard Lindon") (seen in 1880) is believed to have invented the first footballs with rubber bladders.

In Europe, early footballs were made out of animal [bladders](/wiki/Urinary_bladder "Urinary bladder"), more specifically [pig's bladders](/wiki/Pig_bladder "Pig bladder"), which were inflated. Later leather coverings were introduced to allow the balls to keep their shape.[[94]](#cite_note-94) However, in 1851, [Richard Lindon](/wiki/Richard_Lindon "Richard Lindon") and [William Gilbert](/wiki/William_Gilbert_(Rugby) "William Gilbert (Rugby)"), both shoemakers from the town of [Rugby](/wiki/Rugby,_Warwickshire "Rugby, Warwickshire") (near the school), exhibited both round and oval-shaped balls at the [Great Exhibition](/wiki/Great_Exhibition "Great Exhibition") in London. Richard Lindon's wife is said to have died of lung disease caused by blowing up pig's bladders.[[a]](#cite_note-97) Lindon also won medals for the invention of the "Rubber inflatable Bladder" and the "Brass Hand Pump".
In 1855, the U.S. inventor [Charles Goodyear](/wiki/Charles_Goodyear "Charles Goodyear") – who had patented [vulcanised rubber](/wiki/Vulcanized_rubber "Vulcanized rubber") – exhibited a spherical football, with an exterior of vulcanised rubber panels, at the [Paris *Exhibition Universelle*](/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1855) "Exposition Universelle (1855)"). The ball was to prove popular in early forms of football in the U.S.[[97]](#cite_note-98)
The iconic ball with a regular pattern of hexagons and pentagons (see [truncated icosahedron](/wiki/Truncated_icosahedron "Truncated icosahedron")) did not become popular until the 1960s, and was first used in the World Cup [in 1970](/wiki/1970_FIFA_World_Cup "1970 FIFA World Cup").

#### Modern ball passing tactics

Main article: [Passing (association football)](/wiki/Passing_(association_football) "Passing (association football)")

The earliest reference to a game of football involving players passing the ball and attempting to score past a goalkeeper was written in 1633 by David Wedderburn, a poet and teacher in [Aberdeen](/wiki/Aberdeen "Aberdeen"), Scotland.[[98]](#cite_note-99) Nevertheless, the original text does not state whether the allusion to passing as 'kick the ball back' ('repercute pilam') was in a forward or backward direction or between members of the same opposing teams (as was usual at this time).[[99]](#cite_note-100)
"Scientific" football is first recorded in 1839 from [Lancashire](/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire")[[100]](#cite_note-101) and in the modern game in rugby football from 1862[[101]](#cite_note-102) and from Sheffield FC as early as 1865.[[102]](#cite_note-103)[[103]](#cite_note-104) The first side to play a passing [combination game](/wiki/Combination_game "Combination game") was the [Royal Engineers AFC](/wiki/Royal_Engineers_AFC "Royal Engineers AFC") in 1869/70.[[104]](#cite_note-105)[[105]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-106) By 1869 they were "work[ing] well together", "backing up" and benefiting from "cooperation".[[106]](#cite_note-107) By 1870 the Engineers were passing the ball: "Lieut. Creswell, who having brought the ball up the side then kicked it into the middle to another of his side, who kicked it through the posts the minute before time was called".[[107]](#cite_note-108) Passing was a regular feature of their style.[[108]](#cite_note-109) By early 1872 the Engineers were the first football team renowned for "play[ing] beautifully together".[[109]](#cite_note-110) A double pass is first reported from Derby school against [Nottingham Forest](/wiki/Nottingham_Forest "Nottingham Forest") in March 1872, the first of which is irrefutably a *short* pass: "Mr Absey dribbling the ball half the length of the field delivered it to Wallis, who kicking it cleverly in front of the goal, sent it to the captain who drove it at once between the Nottingham posts".[[110]](#cite_note-111) The first side to have perfected the modern formation was [Cambridge University AFC](/wiki/Cambridge_University_AFC "Cambridge University AFC");[[111]](#cite_note-112)[[112]](#cite_note-113)[[113]](#cite_note-114) they also introduced the 2–3–5 "pyramid" formation.[[114]](#cite_note-115)[[115]](#cite_note-116)

### Rugby football

Main articles: [Rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") and [History of rugby union](/wiki/History_of_rugby_union "History of rugby union")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Last_scrimmage_buckman.jpg/250px-Last_scrimmage_buckman.jpg)](/wiki/File:Last_scrimmage_buckman.jpg)

*The Last Scrimmage* by Edwin Buckman, depicting a rugby scrum in 1871

Rugby football was thought to have been started about 1845 at [Rugby School](/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School") in [Rugby, Warwickshire](/wiki/Rugby,_Warwickshire "Rugby, Warwickshire"), England although forms of football in which the ball was carried and tossed date to [medieval](/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") times. In [Britain](/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland"), by 1870, there were 49 clubs playing variations of the Rugby school game.[[116]](#cite_note-117) There were also "rugby" clubs in Ireland, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. However, there was no generally accepted set of rules for rugby until 1871, when 21 clubs from London came together to form the [Rugby Football Union](/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union") (RFU). The first official RFU rules were adopted in June 1871.[[117]](#cite_note-118) These rules allowed passing the ball. They also included the [try](/wiki/Try_(rugby) "Try (rugby)"), where touching the ball over the line allowed an attempt at goal, though drop-goals from marks and general play, and penalty conversions were still the main form of contest. Regardless of any form of football, the first international match between the national team of England and [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") took place at Raeburn Place on 27 March 1871.
[Rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") split into [Rugby union](/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"), [Rugby league](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"), [American football](/wiki/American_football "American football"), and [Canadian football](/wiki/Canadian_football "Canadian football"). [Tom Wills](/wiki/Tom_Wills "Tom Wills") played Rugby football in England before founding [Australian rules football](/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football").

### Cambridge rules

Main article: [Cambridge rules](/wiki/Cambridge_rules "Cambridge rules")

During the nineteenth century, several codifications of the rules of football were made at the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), to enable students from different public schools to play each other. The Cambridge Rules of 1863 influenced the decision of the [Football Association](/wiki/Football_Association "Football Association") to ban Rugby-style carrying of the ball in its own first set of laws.[[118]](#cite_note-119)

### Sheffield rules

Main article: [Sheffield rules](/wiki/Sheffield_rules "Sheffield rules")

By the late 1850s, many football clubs had been formed throughout the English-speaking world, to play various codes of football. [Sheffield Football Club](/wiki/Sheffield_F.C. "Sheffield F.C."), founded in 1857 in the English city of [Sheffield](/wiki/Sheffield "Sheffield") by Nathaniel Creswick and William Prest, was later recognised as the world's oldest club playing association football.[[119]](#cite_note-Football,_the_First_Hundred_Years-120)
However, the club initially played its own code of football: the *Sheffield rules*. The code was largely independent of the public school rules, the most significant difference being the lack of an *offside* rule.
The code was responsible for many innovations that later spread to association football. These included [free kicks](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/free_kick "wikt:free kick"), [corner kicks](/wiki/Corner_kick "Corner kick"), handball, [throw-ins](/wiki/Throw-in "Throw-in") and the crossbar.[[120]](#cite_note-121) By the 1870s they became the dominant code in the north and midlands of England. At this time, a series of rule changes by both the [London](/wiki/The_Football_Association "The Football Association") and [Sheffield](/wiki/Sheffield_and_Hallamshire_County_Football_Association "Sheffield and Hallamshire County Football Association") FAs gradually eroded the differences between the two games until the adoption of a common code in 1877.

### Australian rules football

Main article: [Australian rules football](/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football")

See also: [Origins of Australian rules football](/wiki/Origins_of_Australian_rules_football "Origins of Australian rules football")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Tom_Wills_1857.jpg/250px-Tom_Wills_1857.jpg)](/wiki/File:Tom_Wills_1857.jpg)

[Tom Wills](/wiki/Tom_Wills "Tom Wills"), major figure in the creation of Australian football

There is archival evidence of "foot-ball" games being played in various parts of Australia throughout the first half of the 19th century. The origins of an organised game of football known today as Australian rules football can be traced back to 1858 in [Melbourne](/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), the capital city of [Victoria](/wiki/Victoria_(state) "Victoria (state)").
In July 1858, [Tom Wills](/wiki/Tom_Wills "Tom Wills"), an Australian-born [cricketer](/wiki/Cricketer "Cricketer") educated at [Rugby School](/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School") in England, wrote a letter to *[Bell's Life in Victoria](/wiki/Bell%27s_Life_in_Victoria "Bell's Life in Victoria") & Sporting Chronicle*, calling for a "foot-ball club" with a "code of laws" to keep cricketers fit during winter.[[121]](#cite_note-122) This is considered by historians to be a defining moment in the creation of Australian rules football. Through publicity and personal contacts Wills was able to co-ordinate football matches in Melbourne that experimented with various rules,[[122]](#cite_note-Origins-123) the first of which was played on 31 July 1858. One week later, Wills umpired a schoolboys match between [Melbourne Grammar School](/wiki/Melbourne_Grammar_School "Melbourne Grammar School") and [Scotch College](/wiki/Scotch_College_(Melbourne) "Scotch College (Melbourne)"). Following these matches, organised football in Melbourne rapidly increased in popularity.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Australianfootball1866.jpg/250px-Australianfootball1866.jpg)](/wiki/File:Australianfootball1866.jpg)

Wood engraving of an Australian rules football match at the [Richmond Paddock](/wiki/Yarra_Park "Yarra Park"), [Melbourne](/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), 1866

Wills and others involved in these early matches formed the [Melbourne Football Club](/wiki/Melbourne_Football_Club "Melbourne Football Club") (the oldest surviving Australian football club) on 14 May 1859. Club members Wills, [William Hammersley](/wiki/William_Hammersley "William Hammersley"), [J. B. Thompson](/wiki/J._B._Thompson "J. B. Thompson") and [Thomas H. Smith](/wiki/Thomas_H._Smith "Thomas H. Smith") met with the intention of forming a set of rules that would be widely adopted by other clubs. The committee debated rules used in English public school games; Wills pushed for various [rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") rules he learnt during his schooling. The first rules share similarities with these games, and were shaped to suit to Australian conditions. [H. C. A. Harrison](/wiki/H._C._A._Harrison "H. C. A. Harrison"), a seminal figure in Australian football, recalled that his cousin Wills wanted "a game of our own".[[123]](#cite_note-124) The code was distinctive in the prevalence of the [mark](/wiki/Mark_(Australian_football) "Mark (Australian football)"), [free kick](/wiki/Free_kick_(Australian_rules_football) "Free kick (Australian rules football)"), [tackling](/wiki/Tackle_(football_move)#Australian_rules_football "Tackle (football move)"), lack of an offside rule and that players were specifically penalised for [throwing the ball](/wiki/Handball_(Australian_rules_football) "Handball (Australian rules football)").
The Melbourne football rules were widely distributed and gradually adopted by the other Victorian clubs. The rules were updated several times during the 1860s to accommodate the rules of other influential Victorian football clubs. A significant redraft in 1866 by H. C. A. Harrison's committee accommodated the [Geelong Football Club](/wiki/Geelong_Football_Club "Geelong Football Club")'s rules, making the game then known as "Victorian Rules" increasingly distinct from other codes. It soon adopted [cricket fields](/wiki/Cricket_field "Cricket field") and an oval ball, used specialised goal and behind posts, and featured [bouncing the ball while running](/wiki/Running_bounce "Running bounce") and [spectacular high marking](/wiki/Specky "Specky"). The game spread quickly to other [Australian colonies](/wiki/Australian_states_and_territories "Australian states and territories"). Outside its heartland in southern Australia, the code experienced a significant period of decline following World War I but has since grown throughout Australia and in [other parts of the world](/wiki/Australian_football_around_the_world "Australian football around the world"), and the [Australian Football League](/wiki/Australian_Football_League "Australian Football League") emerged as the dominant professional competition.

### The Football Association

Main article: [The Football Association](/wiki/The_Football_Association "The Football Association")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/1872_engl_v_scotland_ralston.jpg/250px-1872_engl_v_scotland_ralston.jpg)](/wiki/File:1872_engl_v_scotland_ralston.jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/1872_engl_v_scotland-2.jpg/250px-1872_engl_v_scotland-2.jpg)](/wiki/File:1872_engl_v_scotland-2.jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/1872_engl_v_scotland-3.jpg/120px-1872_engl_v_scotland-3.jpg)](/wiki/File:1872_engl_v_scotland-3.jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/1872_engl_v_scotland-4.jpg/250px-1872_engl_v_scotland-4.jpg)](/wiki/File:1872_engl_v_scotland-4.jpg)

The first [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") international, [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland_national_football_team "Scotland national football team") versus [England](/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team"). Once kept by the [Rugby Football Union](/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union") as an early example of [rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football").

During the early 1860s, there were increasing attempts in England to unify and reconcile the various public school games. In 1862, J. C. Thring, who had been one of the driving forces behind the original Cambridge Rules, was a master at [Uppingham School](/wiki/Uppingham_School "Uppingham School"), and he issued his own rules of what he called "The Simplest Game" (these are also known as the Uppingham Rules). In early October 1863, another new revised version of the Cambridge Rules was drawn up by a seven member committee representing former pupils from Harrow, Shrewsbury, Eton, Rugby, Marlborough and Westminster.
At the [Freemasons' Tavern](/wiki/Freemasons%27_Tavern "Freemasons' Tavern"), Great Queen Street, London on the evening of 26 October 1863, representatives of several football clubs in the [London Metropolitan area](/wiki/County_of_London "County of London") met for the inaugural meeting of the [Football Association](/wiki/The_Football_Association "The Football Association") (FA). The aim of the association was to establish a single unifying code and regulate the playing of the game among its members. Following the first meeting, the public schools were invited to join the association. All of them declined, except Charterhouse and Uppingham. In total, six meetings of the FA were held between October and December 1863. After the third meeting, a draft set of rules was published. However, at the beginning of the fourth meeting, attention was drawn to the recently published Cambridge Rules of 1863. The Cambridge rules differed from the draft FA rules in two significant areas; namely running with (carrying) the ball and [hacking](/wiki/Hacking_(rugby) "Hacking (rugby)") (kicking opposing players in the shins). The two contentious FA rules were as follows:

> IX. A player shall be entitled to run with the ball towards his adversaries' goal if he makes a fair catch, or catches the ball on the first bound; but in case of a fair catch, if he makes his mark he shall not run.
>
> X. If any player shall run with the ball towards his adversaries' goal, any player on the opposite side shall be at liberty to charge, hold, trip or hack him, or to wrest the ball from him, but no player shall be held and hacked at the same time.[[124]](#cite_note-125)

At the fifth meeting it was proposed that these two rules be removed. Most of the delegates supported this, but [F. M. Campbell](/wiki/F._M._Campbell "F. M. Campbell"), the representative from [Blackheath](/wiki/Blackheath_Rugby_Club "Blackheath Rugby Club") and the first FA treasurer, objected. He said: "hacking is the true football". However, the motion to ban running with the ball in hand and hacking was carried and Blackheath withdrew from the FA. After the final meeting on 8 December, the FA published the "[Laws of the Game](/wiki/Laws_of_the_Game_(association_football) "Laws of the Game (association football)")", the first comprehensive set of rules for the game later known as association football. The term "soccer", in use since the late 19th century, derives from an [Oxford University abbreviation](/wiki/Oxford_%22-er%22 "Oxford \"-er\"") of "association".[[125]](#cite_note-OEDsoccer-126)
The first FA rules still contained elements that are no longer part of association football, but which are still recognisable in other games (such as Australian football and rugby football): for instance, a player could make a fair catch and claim a *[mark](/wiki/Mark_(Australian_football) "Mark (Australian football)")*, which entitled him to a free kick; and if a player touched the ball behind the opponents' goal line, his side was entitled to a *free kick* at goal, from 15 yards (13.5 metres) in front of the goal line.

### North American football codes

Main articles: [Gridiron football](/wiki/Gridiron_football "Gridiron football"), [History of American football](/wiki/History_of_American_football "History of American football"), and [Canadian football § History](/wiki/Canadian_football#History "Canadian football")

As was the case in Britain, by the early 19th century, North American schools and universities played their own local games, between sides made up of students. For example, students at [Dartmouth College](/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College") in [New Hampshire](/wiki/New_Hampshire "New Hampshire") played a game called [Old division football](/wiki/Old_division_football "Old division football"), a variant of the association football codes, as early as the 1820s.[[62]](#cite_note-ODF-62) They remained largely "[mob football](/wiki/Mob_football "Mob football")" style games, with huge numbers of players attempting to advance the ball into a goal area, often by any means necessary. Rules were simple, violence and injury were common.[[61]](#cite_note-PFRA1-61) The violence of these mob-style games led to widespread protests and a decision to abandon them. [Yale University](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), under pressure from the city of [New Haven](/wiki/New_Haven,_Connecticut "New Haven, Connecticut"), banned the play of all forms of football in 1860, while [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") followed suit in 1861.[[61]](#cite_note-PFRA1-61) In its place, two general types of football evolved: "kicking" games and "running" (or "carrying") games. A hybrid of the two, known as the "[Boston game](/wiki/Boston_game "Boston game")", was played by a group known as the [Oneida Football Club](/wiki/Oneida_Football_Club "Oneida Football Club"). The club, considered by some historians as the first formal [football club](/wiki/Football_club "Football club") in the United States, was formed in 1862 by schoolboys who played the Boston game on [Boston Common](/wiki/Boston_Common "Boston Common").[[61]](#cite_note-PFRA1-61)[[126]](#cite_note-127) The game began to return to American college campuses by the late 1860s. The universities of Yale, [Princeton](/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University") (then known as the College of New Jersey), [Rutgers](/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University"), and [Brown](/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University") all began playing "kicking" games during this time. In 1867, Princeton used rules based on those of the English [Football Association](/wiki/The_Football_Association "The Football Association").[[61]](#cite_note-PFRA1-61)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/The_Tigers_of_Hamilton_football_team.jpg/250px-The_Tigers_of_Hamilton_football_team.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_Tigers_of_Hamilton_football_team.jpg)

The Tigers of [Hamilton, Ontario](/wiki/Hamilton,_Ontario "Hamilton, Ontario"), circa 1906. Founded 1869 as the Hamilton Foot Ball Club, they eventually merged with the Hamilton Flying Wildcats to form the [Hamilton Tiger-Cats](/wiki/Hamilton_Tiger-Cats "Hamilton Tiger-Cats"), a team still active in the [Canadian Football League](/wiki/Canadian_Football_League "Canadian Football League").[[127]](#cite_note-Football_Canada_timeline-128)

In Canada, the first documented football match was a practice game played on 9 November 1861, at [University College, University of Toronto](/wiki/University_College,_University_of_Toronto "University College, University of Toronto") (approximately 400 yards west of Queen's Park). One of the participants in the game involving University of Toronto students was (Sir) William Mulock, later Chancellor of the school.[[128]](#cite_note-1860s-129) In 1864, at [Trinity College](/wiki/University_of_Trinity_College "University of Trinity College"), Toronto, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn, one of the founders of Milton, Massachusetts, devised rules based on [rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football").[[128]](#cite_note-1860s-129) A "running game", resembling rugby football, was then taken up by the [Montreal Football Club](/wiki/Montreal_Football_Club "Montreal Football Club") in Canada in 1868.[[129]](#cite_note-histfoot-130)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/1882RutgersFootballTeam.jpg/250px-1882RutgersFootballTeam.jpg)](/wiki/File:1882RutgersFootballTeam.jpg)

Rutgers University (here pictured in 1882) played the first inter-collegiate football game v Princeton in 1869.

On 6 November 1869, [Rutgers](/wiki/Rutgers_Scarlet_Knights_football "Rutgers Scarlet Knights football") faced [Princeton](/wiki/Princeton_Tigers_football "Princeton Tigers football") in a game that was played with a round ball and, like all early games, used improvised rules. It is usually regarded as [the first game of American intercollegiate football](/wiki/1869_New_Jersey_vs._Rutgers_football_game "1869 New Jersey vs. Rutgers football game").[[61]](#cite_note-PFRA1-61)[[130]](#cite_note-131)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/HarvardMcGill.jpg/250px-HarvardMcGill.jpg)](/wiki/File:HarvardMcGill.jpg)

The Harvard v McGill game in 1874. It is considered the first rugby football game played in the United States.

Modern North American football grew out of [a match](/wiki/1874_Harvard_vs._McGill_football_game "1874 Harvard vs. McGill football game") between [McGill University](/wiki/McGill_Redmen_football "McGill Redmen football") of Montreal and [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_Crimson_football "Harvard Crimson football") in 1874. During the game, the two teams alternated between the rugby-based rules used by McGill and the Boston Game rules used by Harvard.[[131]](#cite_note-132)[[132]](#cite_note-133)[[133]](#cite_note-134) Within a few years, Harvard had both adopted McGill's rules and persuaded other U.S. university teams to do the same. On 23 November 1876, representatives from Harvard, Yale, Princeton, and [Columbia](/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") met at the Massasoit Convention in [Springfield, Massachusetts](/wiki/Springfield,_Massachusetts "Springfield, Massachusetts"), agreeing to adopt most of the [Rugby Football Union](/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union") rules, with some variations.[[134]](#cite_note-PFRA2-135)
In 1880, [Yale](/wiki/Yale_Bulldogs_football "Yale Bulldogs football") coach [Walter Camp](/wiki/Walter_Camp "Walter Camp"), who had become a fixture at the Massasoit House conventions where the rules were debated and changed, devised a number of major innovations. Camp's two most important rule changes that diverged the American game from rugby were replacing the [scrummage](/wiki/Scrum_(rugby) "Scrum (rugby)") with the *[line of scrimmage](/wiki/Line_of_scrimmage "Line of scrimmage")* and the establishment of the *[down-and-distance](/wiki/Down_(American_and_Canadian_football) "Down (American and Canadian football)")* rules.[[134]](#cite_note-PFRA2-135) American football still however remained a violent sport where collisions often led to serious injuries and sometimes even death.[[135]](#cite_note-136) This led U.S. President [Theodore Roosevelt](/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") to hold a meeting with football representatives from Harvard, Yale, and Princeton on 9 October 1905, urging them to make drastic changes.[[136]](#cite_note-137) One rule change introduced in 1906, devised to open up the game and reduce injury, was the introduction of the legal [forward pass](/wiki/Forward_pass "Forward pass"). Though it was underused for years, this proved to be one of the most important rule changes in the establishment of the modern game.[[137]](#cite_note-138)
Over the years, Canada absorbed some of the developments in American football in an effort to distinguish it from a more rugby-oriented game. In 1903, the [Ontario Rugby Football Union](/wiki/Ontario_Rugby_Football_Union "Ontario Rugby Football Union") adopted the [Burnside rules](/wiki/Burnside_rules "Burnside rules"), which implemented the *line of scrimmage* and *down-and-distance* system from American football, among others.[[138]](#cite_note-139) Canadian football then implemented the legal forward pass in 1929.[[139]](#cite_note-140) American and Canadian football [remain different codes](/wiki/Comparison_of_American_and_Canadian_football "Comparison of American and Canadian football"), stemming from rule changes that the American side of the border adopted but the Canadian side has not.

### Gaelic football

Main article: [History of Gaelic football](/wiki/Gaelic_football#History "Gaelic football")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Croke_Park_from_the_Hill_-_2004_All-Ireland_Football_Championship_Final.jpg/330px-Croke_Park_from_the_Hill_-_2004_All-Ireland_Football_Championship_Final.jpg)](/wiki/File:Croke_Park_from_the_Hill_-_2004_All-Ireland_Football_Championship_Final.jpg)

The [All-Ireland Football Final](/wiki/All-Ireland_Senior_Football_Championship "All-Ireland Senior Football Championship") in [Croke Park](/wiki/Croke_Park "Croke Park"), 2004

In the mid-19th century, various traditional football games, referred to collectively as *[caid](/wiki/Caid_(sport) "Caid (sport)")*, remained popular in Ireland, especially in [County Kerry](/wiki/County_Kerry "County Kerry"). One observer, Father W. Ferris, described two main forms of *caid* during this period: the "field game" in which the object was to put the ball through arch-like goals, formed from the boughs of two trees; and the epic "cross-country game" which took up most of the daylight hours of a Sunday on which it was played, and was won by one team taking the ball across a parish boundary. "Wrestling", "holding" opposing players, and carrying the ball were all allowed.
By the 1870s, rugby and association football had started to become popular in Ireland. [Trinity College Dublin](/wiki/Trinity_College_Dublin "Trinity College Dublin") was an early stronghold of rugby (see the [Developments in the 1850s](#Other_developments_in_the_1850s) section above). The rules of the English FA were being distributed widely. Traditional forms of *caid* had begun to give way to a "rough-and-tumble game" which allowed tripping.
There was no serious attempt to unify and codify Irish varieties of football, until the establishment of the [Gaelic Athletic Association](/wiki/Gaelic_Athletic_Association "Gaelic Athletic Association") (GAA) in 1884. The GAA sought to promote traditional Irish sports, such as [hurling](/wiki/Hurling "Hurling") and to reject imported games like rugby and association football. The first Gaelic football rules were drawn up by [Maurice Davin](/wiki/Maurice_Davin "Maurice Davin") and published in the *United Ireland* magazine on 7 February 1887.[[140]](#cite_note-141) Davin's rules showed the influence of games such as hurling and a desire to formalise a distinctly Irish code of football. The prime example of this differentiation was the lack of an offside rule (an attribute which, for many years, was shared only by other Irish games like hurling, and by Australian rules football).

### Schism in Rugby football

Further information: [History of rugby league](/wiki/History_of_rugby_league "History of rugby league")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Reverend_marshall.jpg/250px-Reverend_marshall.jpg)](/wiki/File:Reverend_marshall.jpg)

An English cartoon from the 1890s lampooning the divide in rugby football which led to the formation of [rugby league](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"). The caricatures are of Rev. Frank Marshall, an arch-opponent of player payments, and James Miller, a long-time opponent of Marshall. The caption reads: Marshall: "Oh, fie, go away naughty boy, I don't play with boys who can't afford to take a holiday for football any day they like!" Miller: "Yes, that's just you to a T; you'd make it so that no lad whose father wasn't a millionaire could play at all in a really good team. For my part I see no reason why the men who make the money shouldn't have a share in the spending of it."

The [International Rugby Football Board](/wiki/International_Rugby_Board "International Rugby Board") (IRFB) was founded in 1886,[[141]](#cite_note-142) but rifts were beginning to emerge in the code. [Professionalism](/wiki/Professional_sports "Professional sports") had already begun to creep into the various codes of football.
In England, by the 1890s, a long-standing [Rugby Football Union](/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union") ban on *professional* players was causing regional tensions within rugby football, as many players in northern England were working class and could not afford to take time off to train, travel, play and recover from injuries. This was not very different from what had occurred ten years earlier in soccer in Northern England but the authorities reacted very differently in the RFU, attempting to alienate the working class support in Northern England. In 1895, following a dispute about a player being paid broken time payments, which replaced wages lost as a result of playing rugby, representatives of the northern clubs met in [Huddersfield](/wiki/Huddersfield "Huddersfield") to form the [Northern Rugby Football Union](/wiki/Rugby_Football_League "Rugby Football League") (NRFU). The new body initially permitted only various types of player wage replacements. However, within two years, NRFU players could be paid, but they were required to have a job outside sport.[[142]](#cite_note-schism-143)
The demands of a professional league dictated that rugby had to become a better "spectator" sport. Within a few years the NRFU rules had started to diverge from the RFU, most notably with the abolition of the *[line-out](/wiki/Line-out_(rugby_union) "Line-out (rugby union)")*. This was followed by the replacement of the *[ruck](/wiki/Playing_rugby_union#Ruck "Playing rugby union")* with the "play-the-ball ruck", which allowed a two-player ruck contest between the tackler at marker and the player tackled. *[Mauls](/wiki/Rugby_union_gameplay#Maul "Rugby union gameplay")* were stopped once the ball carrier was held, being replaced by a play-the ball-ruck. The separate Lancashire and Yorkshire competitions of the NRFU merged in 1901, forming the Northern Rugby League, the first time the name [rugby league](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league") was used officially in England.[[142]](#cite_note-schism-143)
Over time, the RFU form of rugby, played by clubs which remained members of national federations affiliated to the IRFB, became known as [rugby union](/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union").[[142]](#cite_note-schism-143)

### Globalisation of association football

Main article: [History of FIFA](/wiki/History_of_FIFA "History of FIFA")

The need for a single body to oversee association football had become apparent by the beginning of the 20th century, with the increasing popularity of international fixtures. The English Football Association had chaired many discussions on setting up an international body, but was perceived as making no progress. It fell to associations from seven other European countries: France, Belgium, Denmark, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland, to form an international association. The *Fédération Internationale de Football Association* ([FIFA](/wiki/FIFA "FIFA")) was founded in Paris on 21 May 1904.[[143]](#cite_note-FIFA.com-144) Its first president was [Robert Guérin](/wiki/Robert_Gu%C3%A9rin "Robert Guérin").[[143]](#cite_note-FIFA.com-144) The French name and acronym has remained, even outside French-speaking countries.

### Further divergence of the two rugby codes

Rugby league rules diverged significantly from rugby union in 1906, with the reduction of the team from 15 to 13 players. In 1907, a New Zealand professional rugby team toured Australia and Britain, receiving an enthusiastic response, and professional [rugby leagues were launched in Australia](/wiki/Rugby_league_in_Australia "Rugby league in Australia") the following year. However, the rules of professional games varied from one country to another, and negotiations between various national bodies were required to fix the exact rules for each international match. This situation endured until 1948, when at the instigation of the French league, the [Rugby League International Federation](/wiki/Rugby_League_International_Federation "Rugby League International Federation") (RLIF) was formed at a meeting in [Bordeaux](/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux").
During the second half of the 20th century, the rules changed further. In 1966, rugby league officials borrowed the American football concept of *[downs](/wiki/Down_(football) "Down (football)")*: a team was allowed to retain possession of the ball for four tackles (rugby union retains the original rule that a player who is tackled and brought to the ground must release the ball immediately). The maximum number of tackles was later increased to six (in 1971), and in rugby league this became known as the *[six tackle rule](/wiki/Playing_rugby_league#Six_tackle_rule "Playing rugby league")*.
With the advent of full-time professionals in the early 1990s, and the consequent speeding up of the game, the five-metre off-side distance between the two teams became 10 metres, and the replacement rule was superseded by various interchange rules, among other changes.
The laws of rugby union also changed during the 20th century, although less significantly than those of rugby league. In particular, goals from *[marks](/wiki/Mark_(rugby) "Mark (rugby)")* were abolished, kicks directly *[into touch](/wiki/Touch_(rugby) "Touch (rugby)")* from outside the *[22-metre](/wiki/Rugby_pitch "Rugby pitch")* line were penalised, new laws were put in place to determine who had possession following an inconclusive *[ruck](/wiki/Ruck_(Rugby_union) "Ruck (Rugby union)")* or *[maul](/wiki/Rugby_union_gameplay#Maul "Rugby union gameplay")*, and the lifting of players in *[line-outs](/wiki/Line-out_(rugby_union) "Line-out (rugby union)")* was legalised.
In 1995, rugby union became an "open" game, that is one which allowed professional players.[[144]](#cite_note-145) Although the original dispute between the two codes has now disappeared – and despite the fact that officials from both forms of rugby football have sometimes mentioned the possibility of re-unification – the rules of both codes and their culture have diverged to such an extent that such an event is unlikely in the foreseeable future.

Use of the word *football*
--------------------------

Further information: [Football (word)](/wiki/Football_(word) "Football (word)")

The word *football*, when used in reference to a specific game can mean any one of those described above. Because of this, much controversy has occurred over the term *football*, primarily because it is used in different ways in different parts of the [English-speaking world](/wiki/English-speaking_world "English-speaking world"). Most often, the word *football* is used to refer to the code of football that is considered dominant within a particular region (which is association football in most countries). So, effectively, what the word *football* means usually depends on where one says it.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/The_Sportsman_1910-11-25_Football.png/250px-The_Sportsman_1910-11-25_Football.png)](/wiki/File:The_Sportsman_1910-11-25_Football.png)

Heading from The Sportsman (London) front page of 25 November 1910, illustrating the continued use of the word "football" to encompass both association football and rugby

In each of the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada, one football code is known solely as *football*, while the others generally require a qualifier. In New Zealand, *football* historically referred to [rugby union](/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"), but more recently may be used unqualified to refer to association football. The sport meant by the word *football* in Australia is either [Australian rules football](/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football") or [rugby league](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"), depending on local popularity (which largely conforms to the [Barassi Line](/wiki/Barassi_Line "Barassi Line")). In [francophone](/wiki/Francophone "Francophone") [Quebec](/wiki/Quebec "Quebec"), where [Canadian football](/wiki/Canadian_football "Canadian football") is more popular, the Canadian code is known as *le football* while American football is known as *le football américain* and association football is known as *le soccer*.[[145]](#cite_note-146)
Of the 45 national [FIFA](/wiki/FIFA "FIFA") (Fédération Internationale de Football Association) affiliates in which English is an official or primary language, most currently use *Football* in their organisations' official names; the FIFA affiliates in [Canada](/wiki/Canadian_Soccer_Association "Canadian Soccer Association") and the [United States](/wiki/United_States_Soccer_Federation "United States Soccer Federation") use *Soccer* in their names. A few FIFA affiliates have recently "normalised" to using *Football*, including:

* [Australia's association football governing body](/wiki/Football_Federation_Australia "Football Federation Australia") changed its name in 2005 from using *soccer* to *football*.[[146]](#cite_note-147)
* [New Zealand's governing body](/wiki/New_Zealand_Football "New Zealand Football") renamed itself in 2007, saying "the international game is called football".[[147]](#cite_note-148)
* Samoa changed from "Samoa Football (Soccer) Federation" to "[Football Federation Samoa](/wiki/Football_Federation_Samoa "Football Federation Samoa")" in 2009.[[148]](#cite_note-149)[[149]](#cite_note-150)

Small football stadium in [Croatia](/wiki/Croatia "Croatia")

Several of the football codes are the most popular team sports in the world.[[12]](#cite_note-Bale-12) Globally, [association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") is played by States"),[[153]](#cite_note-154)[[154]](#cite_note-Estimated_Probability_of_Competing_in_Athletics_Beyond_the_High_School_Interscholastic_Level-155) with the annual [Super Bowl](/wiki/Super_Bowl     - Minivoetbal – the five-a-side indoor game played in East and West [Flanders](/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") where it is extremely popular

  + [Masters Football](/wiki/Masters_Football "Masters Football") – six-a-side played in Europe by mature professionals (35 years and older)
* [Paralympic football](/wiki/Paralympic_football "Paralympic football") – modified game for athletes with a disability.[[192]](#cite_note-198) Includes:

  + Football 7-a-side – for athletes with [cerebral palsy](/wiki/Cerebral_palsy "Cerebral palsy")
  + Amputee football – for athletes with [amputations](/wiki/Amputation "Amputation")
  + Deaf football – for athletes with [hearing impairments](/wiki/Hearing_impairment "Hearing impairment")
  + [Powerchair football](/wiki/Powerchair_football "Powerchair football") – for athletes in electric wheelchairs

* [Rush goalie](/wiki/Rush_goalie "Rush goalie") – a variation in which the role of the goalkeeper is more flexible than normal
* [Crab football](/wiki/Crab_football "Crab football") – players stand on their hands and feet and move around on their backs whilst playing
* [Swamp soccer](/wiki/Swamp_soccer "Swamp soccer") – the game as played on a [swamp](/wiki/Swamp "Swamp") or [bog](/wiki/Bog "Bog") field
* [Jorkyball](/wiki/Jorkyball "Jorkyball")
* [Walking football](/wiki/Walking_football "Walking football") – players are restricted to walking, to facilitate participation by older and less mobile players

*These codes have in common the ability of players to carry the ball with their hands, and to throw it to teammates, unlike association football where the use of hands during play is prohibited by anyone except the goalkeeper. They also feature various methods of scoring based upon whether the ball is carried into the goal area, or kicked above the goalposts. They are broadly divided into two families:*
*The Rugby codes are notable for a prohibition on passing the ball forwards with the hands*

* [Rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football")
  + [Rugby union](/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union")
    - [Mini rugby](/wiki/Mini_rugby "Mini rugby") a variety for children.
    - [Rugby sevens](/wiki/Rugby_sevens "Rugby sevens") and [Rugby tens](/wiki/Rugby_tens "Rugby tens") – variants for teams of reduced size.
  + [Rugby league](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league") – often referred to simply as "league", and usually known simply as "football" or "footy" in the Australian states of New South Wales and Queensland.
    - [Touch](/wiki/Touch_(sport) "Touch (sport)"), non-contact
    - [Rugby league sevens](/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens "Rugby league sevens") and [Rugby league nines](/wiki/Rugby_league_nines "Rugby league nines") – variants for teams of reduced size.
  + [Beach rugby](/wiki/Beach_rugby "Beach rugby") – rugby played on sand
  + [Touch rugby](/wiki/Touch_rugby "Touch rugby") – generic name for forms of rugby football which do not feature tackles.
  + [Tag Rugby](/wiki/Tag_Rugby "Tag Rugby") – non-contact variant in which a flag attached to a player is removed to indicate a tackle.

*Gridiron codes share a history with rugby codes, but allow some forward passing*

* [Gridiron football](/wiki/Gridiron_football "Gridiron football")
  + [American football](/wiki/American_football "American football") – called "football" in the United States and Canada, and "gridiron" in Australia and New Zealand.
    - [Nine-man football](/wiki/Nine-man_football "Nine-man football"), [eight-man football](/wiki/Eight-man_football "Eight-man football"), [six-man football](/wiki/Six-man_football "Six-man football") – variants played primarily by smaller high schools that lack enough players to field full teams.
    - [Street football](/wiki/Street_football_(American) "Street football (American)")/backyard football – played without equipment or official fields and with simplified rules
    - [Flag football](/wiki/Flag_football "Flag football") – non-contact variant in which a flag attached to a player is removed to indicate a tackle.
    - [Touch football](/wiki/Touch_football_(American) "Touch football (American)") – non-tackle variants
  + [Canadian football](/wiki/Canadian_football "Canadian football") – called simply "football" in Canada; "football" in Canada can mean either Canadian or American football depending on context. All of the variants listed for American football are also attested for Canadian football.
  + [Indoor football](/wiki/Indoor_American_football "Indoor American football") – indoor variants, particularly [arena football](/wiki/Arena_football "Arena football")
  + [Wheelchair football](/wiki/Wheelchair_Football_(American) "Wheelchair Football (American)") – variant adapted to play by athletes with [physical disabilities](/wiki/Physical_disability "Physical disability")

*These codes have in common the absence of a full offside rule and the subsequent man-to-man nature of defending, the prohibition of continuous carrying of the ball (requiring a periodic bounce or solo (toe-kick), depending on the code) while running, handpassing by punching or tapping the ball rather than throwing it, a major and minor scoring system, and other traditions.*

* [Australian rules football](/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football") – officially known as "Australian football", and informally as "football", "footy" or "Aussie rules". In some areas it is referred to as "[AFL](/wiki/Australian_Football_League "Australian Football League")", the name of the main organising body and competition
  + [Auskick](/wiki/Auskick "Auskick") – a version of Australian rules designed by the AFL for young children
  + [Metro footy](/wiki/Metro_footy "Metro footy") (or Metro rules footy) – a modified version invented by the [USAFL](/wiki/United_States_Australian_Football_League "United States Australian Football League"), for use on [gridiron](/wiki/Gridiron_football "Gridiron football") fields in North American cities (which often lack grounds large enough for conventional Australian rules matches)
  + [Kick-to-kick](/wiki/Kick-to-kick "Kick-to-kick") – informal versions of the game
  + [9-a-side footy](/wiki/9-a-side_footy "9-a-side footy") – a more open, running variety of Australian rules, requiring 18 players in total and a proportionally smaller playing area (includes contact and non-contact varieties)
  + [Rec footy](/wiki/Rec_footy "Rec footy") – "Recreational Football", a modified non-contact variation of Australian rules, created by the AFL, which replaces tackles with tags
  + [Touch Aussie Rules](/wiki/Touch_Aussie_Rules "Touch Aussie Rules") – a non-tackle variation of Australian Rules played only in the United Kingdom
  + [Samoa rules](/wiki/Samoa_rules "Samoa rules") – localised version adapted to Samoan conditions, such as the use of [rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") fields
  + [Masters Australian football](/wiki/Masters_Australian_football "Masters Australian football") (a.k.a. *Superules*) – reduced contact version introduced for competitions limited to players over 30 years of age
  + [Women's Australian rules football](/wiki/Women%27s_Australian_rules_football "Women's Australian rules football") – women's competition played with a smaller ball and (sometimes) reduced contact
* [Gaelic football](/wiki/Gaelic_football "Gaelic football") – Played predominantly in Ireland, and abroad by players of Irish extraction or heritage. Commonly referred to as "football", "GAA" or "Gaelic"
  + [Ladies Gaelic football](/wiki/Ladies_Gaelic_football "Ladies Gaelic football")
* [International rules football](/wiki/International_rules_football "International rules football") – a compromise code used for international representative matches between AFL and GAA for Australian rules football players and Gaelic football players

See also: [Comparison of Australian rules football and Gaelic football](/wiki/Comparison_of_Australian_rules_football_and_Gaelic_football "Comparison of Australian rules football and Gaelic football")

### Recent and hybrid

  + [Footbag](/wiki/Footbag "Footbag") – several variations using a small bean bag or sand bag as a ball, the trade marked term [hacky sack](/wiki/Hacky_sack "Hacky sack") is sometimes used as a generic synonym.
  + [Freestyle football](/wiki/Freestyle_football "Freestyle football") – participants are graded for their entertainment value and expression of skill.

#### Association

* [Three sided football](/wiki/Three_sided_football "Three sided football")
* Triskelion

#### Rugby

* [Forceback](/wiki/Forceback "Forceback") a.k.a. **forcing back**, **forcemanback**

#### Hybrid

* [Austus](/wiki/Austus "Austus") – a compromise between Australian rules and [American football](/wiki/American_football "American football"), invented in [Melbourne](/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") during World War II.
* [Speedball](/wiki/Speedball_(American_ball_game) "Speedball (American ball game)") – a combination of American football, soccer, and basketball, devised in the United States in 1912.
* [Universal football](/wiki/Universal_football "Universal football") – a hybrid of Australian rules and rugby league, trialled in Sydney in 1933.[[193]](#cite_note-199)
* [Volata](/wiki/Volata "Volata") – a game resembling association football and [European handball](/wiki/Team_handball "Team handball"), devised by [Italian fascist](/wiki/Italian_fascism "Italian fascism") leader, [Augusto Turati](/wiki/Augusto_Turati "Augusto Turati"), in the 1920s.
* [Wheelchair rugby](/wiki/Wheelchair_rugby "Wheelchair rugby") – also known as **Murderball**, invented in Canada in 1977. Based on [ice hockey](/wiki/Ice_hockey "Ice hockey") and basketball rather than rugby.
* [Underwater football](/wiki/Underwater_football "Underwater football") – played in a pool, and the ball can only be played when underwater. The ball can be carried as in rugby.
* [Roller soccer](/wiki/Roller_soccer "Roller soccer"), a version of association football played on skates.

More distant sports:

* [Cycle ball](/wiki/Cycle_ball "Cycle ball") – a sport similar to association football played on bicycles.
* [Motoball](/wiki/Motoball "Motoball"), [motorcycle team sport](/wiki/Motorcycle_sport "Motorcycle sport") similar to association Football.
* The hockey game [bandy](/wiki/Bandy "Bandy") has rules partly based on the association football rules and is sometimes nicknamed as 'winter football'.

##### Non goal sports

* [Net and wall sports](/wiki/Net_and_wall_games "Net and wall games")
  + [Bossaball](/wiki/Bossaball "Bossaball") – mixes association football and volleyball and gymnastics; played on inflatables and [trampolines](/wiki/Trampoline "Trampoline").
  + [Football tennis](/wiki/Football_tennis "Football tennis") – mixes association football and tennis.
  + [Footvolley](/wiki/Footvolley "Footvolley") – mixes association football and beach volleyball; played on sand.

Although similar to football and volleyball in some aspects, [Sepak takraw](/wiki/Sepak_takraw "Sepak takraw") has ancient origins and cannot be considered a hybrid game. [Teqball](/wiki/Teqball "Teqball"), however, which derives some of its rules and traditions from Sepak takraw, also has hybrid elements.

* Others
  + [Footgolf](/wiki/Footgolf "Footgolf") – golf played by kicking an association football.
  + [Kickball](/wiki/Kickball "Kickball") – a hybrid of association football and baseball, invented in the United States about 1942.

The **Montenegrin Second League** ([Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegrin_language "Montenegrin language"): *Druga crnogorska fudbalska liga* – *Druga CFL* – *2. CFL*) referred to as the **Meridianbet 2. CFL** for sponsorship reasons,[[1]](#cite_note-1) is the second-top [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") league in [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro"). It is headed by the [Football Association of Montenegro](/wiki/Football_Association_of_Montenegro "Football Association of Montenegro"). Second Montenegrin League consists of 10 participants. The top team qualifies for the [First League of Montenegro](/wiki/First_League_of_Montenegro "First League of Montenegro"), the second and third one contest in a playoff match against the 8th and 9th team from the First League, while the bottom-placed two teams are relegated to any of the three [third-tier leagues](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League"), to be replaced by the two winners of a three-way promotion playoffs, contested by the winners of the three Third League divisions.

History
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Before independence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Before independence")]

Main article: [Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946-2006)](/wiki/Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946-2006) "Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946-2006)")

During the existence of [SFR Yugoslavia](/wiki/SFR_Yugoslavia "SFR Yugoslavia"), [FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia "FR Yugoslavia") and [Serbia and Montenegro](/wiki/Serbia_and_Montenegro "Serbia and Montenegro"), from 1947 to 2006, Montenegrin clubs played in federal leagues. Among them, as a second-tier competitions, were [Yugoslav Second League](/wiki/Yugoslav_Second_League "Yugoslav Second League") (1947–1992), [Second League of FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia "Second League of FR Yugoslavia") (1992–2001) and [Second League of Serbia and Montenegro](/wiki/Second_League_of_Serbia_and_Montenegro "Second League of Serbia and Montenegro") (2001–2006).   
Overall, 25 different Montenegrin teams played in Yugoslav Second League from 1947 to 2006. Most seasons in second-tier spent [FK Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") (30), followed by [FK Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") (27) and [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd") (24).

### After independence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: After independence")]

Following [Montenegrin independence referendum (2006)](/wiki/Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 "Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006"), [Football Association of Montenegro](/wiki/Football_Association_of_Montenegro "Football Association of Montenegro") established their own competitions – [First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"), Second League and [Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League").

#### 2006–16

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2006–16")]

On inaugural season [2006–07](/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_Montenegrin_Second_League "2006–07 Montenegrin Second League"), members of Second League became three teams from [Serbia and Montenegro Second League previous season](/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_Montenegrin_First_League "2005–06 Montenegrin First League") and nine from third-tier competition ([Montenegrin Republic League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Republic_League "Montenegrin Republic League")).  
Winner of the first season was [Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") who won the title after the hard struggle with [Ibar](/wiki/FK_Ibar "FK Ibar") and [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj"). Notable game from the season, Ibar – Lovćen (0:1), played in front od 4,000 spectators, finished with crowd disturbances. At the end of the season, Lovćen gained directly promotion to [Prva CFL](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"), while Bokelj won the [playoff](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") games against [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje"). Ibar didn't succeed to gain promotion to Prva CFL.  
[Next year](/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_Montenegrin_Second_League "2007–08 Montenegrin Second League"), the title and directly promotion to highest rank surprisingly gained [FK Jezero](/wiki/FK_Jezero "FK Jezero"), with four points more than [Čelik](/wiki/FK_%C4%8Celik_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Čelik Nikšić"). In the [First League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"), Čelik didn't succeed against their city rivals from [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") in two games which watched 17,000 spectators overall (0:0, 0:1). But, third-placed [FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje") made success in playoff games against [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") (1:0, 0:0) and made a comeback to First League.  
Second League winner for [season 2008–09](/wiki/2008%E2%80%9309_Montenegrin_Second_League "2008–09 Montenegrin Second League") was [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane"), while in the [playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") participated [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd") and [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar"). OFK Titograd lost against [FK Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić"), but Mornar made historical success with their first-ever promotion to Prva CFL after the games against [Jezero](/wiki/FK_Jezero "FK Jezero") (2:1, 0:0). During the season 2008–09, [Otrant](/wiki/FK_Otrant "FK Otrant") scored 12 goals on the match against [Ribnica](/wiki/FK_Ribnica "FK Ribnica") (12:2), which is the all-time record in Montenegrin Second League.  
Title for [2009–10 season](/wiki/2009%E2%80%9310_Montenegrin_Second_League "2009–10 Montenegrin Second League") won [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd"), who made comeback to First League after two seasons. Second-placed [OFK Bar](/wiki/OFK_Bar "OFK Bar") made a surprisingly success in [playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") against [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") after the penalties and made their first and last promotion to Prva CFL. Third-placed [Bratstvo](/wiki/FK_Bratstvo_Cijevna "FK Bratstvo Cijevna") from [Podgorica](/wiki/Podgorica "Podgorica") outskirts lost in playoffs against another team from [Bar](/wiki/Bar,_Montenegro "Bar, Montenegro") – [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") (0:1, 1:2).  
[Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") dominated on [season 2010–11](/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Montenegrin_Second_League "2010–11 Montenegrin Second League"), finishing first with 24 points more than second-placed team. After the [playoff games](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"), promotion to First League gained [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane"), too, while [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje"), which won the second-place, remained in Second League after unsuccessful playoff performances against [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić").  
[Next year](/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Montenegrin_Second_League "2011–12 Montenegrin Second League"), Second League title won [Čelik](/wiki/FK_%C4%8Celik_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Čelik Nikšić") from [Nikšić](/wiki/Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "Nikšić"), with score of 80 points. Except first-ever promotion to the First League in their history, Čelik made notable success in [2011–12 Montenegrin Cup](/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Montenegrin_Cup "2011–12 Montenegrin Cup") during the same season. They became the first member of Second League which played in the finals and won the national Cup. In final game, played in [Podgorica City Stadium](/wiki/Podgorica_City_Stadium "Podgorica City Stadium"), Čelik defeated First-League side [Rudar](/wiki/FK_Rudar_Pljevlja "FK Rudar Pljevlja") – 2:1. Except that, for the first and so far last time in the history, both representatives of Second League won their games in [First League payoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"). Second-placed [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") eliminated [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") (2:1, 3:0), while third-placed [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje") won against [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić") (0:0, 1:0). So, after the season 2011–12, three teams from Second League moved to First League.  
Former elite-member [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić") won the title on [season 2012–13](/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Montenegrin_Second_League "2012–13 Montenegrin Second League") and made a comeback to Prva CFL. Second and third placed [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") and [Zabjelo](/wiki/FK_Zabjelo "FK Zabjelo") lost their games in the playoffs, so only Dečić made a promotion to highest rank. At the beginning of the season, [OFK Bar](/wiki/OFK_Bar "OFK Bar") withdraw due to financial difficulties, so the championship had 11 members.  
After the [edition 2013–14](/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_Montenegrin_Second_League "2013–14 Montenegrin Second League"), [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") and [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") became a members of Prva CFL – Bokelj as title winner and Berane after the playoff games. During that season, on game [Zabjelo](/wiki/FK_Zabjelo "FK Zabjelo") – [Zora](/wiki/FK_Zora "FK Zora") (5–0), player [Bojan Kopitović](/w/index.php?title=Bojan_Kopitovi%C4%87&action=edit&redlink=1 "Bojan Kopitović (page does not exist)") scored five goals, which is the all-time record in Montenegrin Second League.  
On [season 2014–15](/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Montenegrin_Second_League "2014–15 Montenegrin Second League"), title race between [Iskra](/wiki/FK_Iskra_Danilovgrad "FK Iskra Danilovgrad") and [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić") lasted until the end of championship. With two points more than their main opponents, Iskra finished first and made their first-ever promotion to the highest-level competition. But, Dečić gained promotion to Prva CFL too, after the playoff games against former national champions [Mogren](/wiki/FK_Mogren "FK Mogren") (2–1; 5–0).  
[Next year](/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_Montenegrin_Second_League "2015–16 Montenegrin Second League"), [Jedinstvo](/wiki/FK_Jedinstvo_Bijelo_Polje "FK Jedinstvo Bijelo Polje") became a champion. They won the title race with biggest surprise of championship – [Cetinje](/wiki/FK_Cetinje "FK Cetinje"), while the third finished [Bratstvo](/wiki/FK_Bratstvo_Cijevna "FK Bratstvo Cijevna"). But, only Jedinstvo gained promotion. Performances of Cetinje and Bratstvo in playoffs were unsuccessful. That season had 11 members, because [Mogren](/wiki/FK_Mogren "FK Mogren") withdraw due to financial troubles before the start of competition.

#### 2016–

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2016–")]

On [season 2016–17](/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Montenegrin_Second_League "2016–17 Montenegrin Second League"), [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") secured a promotion to Prva CFL after seven years spent in lowest-level competitions. Team from [Podgorica](/wiki/Podgorica "Podgorica") outskirts won the first place, while [Ibar](/wiki/FK_Ibar "FK Ibar") and [Otrant](/wiki/FK_Otrant "FK Otrant") finished second and third, but without promotion.  
[Montenegrin Second League 2017–18](/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Montenegrin_Second_League "2017–18 Montenegrin Second League") finished with success of [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") who won the first place and direct place in [Prva CFL 2018–19](/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Montenegrin_First_League "2018–19 Montenegrin First League"). Third-placed [Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") gained promotion after the playoffs against First-League side [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") (1–0; 0–0), while the newcomer in Second League [FK Podgorica](/wiki/OFK_Mladost_Lje%C5%A1kopolje "OFK Mladost Lješkopolje"), who finished second, lost their playoff games. During the same season, last-placed [Čelik](/wiki/FK_%C4%8Celik_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Čelik Nikšić") made few negative-records at that time. Team which once won the Montenegrin Cup and played in [UEFA Europa League](/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League") finished season with only 8 points, 2 wins, 28 losses, longest run without win (20 games) and one of highest loses in the history of Second League (*[Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj") – Čelik 10–0*).  
[Next year](/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Montenegrin_Second_League "2017–18 Montenegrin Second League"), four weeks before the end of competition, [FK Podgorica](/wiki/OFK_Mladost_Lje%C5%A1kopolje "OFK Mladost Lješkopolje") secured the title and their first ever promotion to the top flight. At the same time, [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") and [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj"), as a second and third placed, participated in the playoffs for First League. As a two last placed teams, [Igalo](/wiki/FK_Igalo "FK Igalo") and [Berane](/wiki/FK_Berane "FK Berane") were relegated to [Montenegrin Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League").  
[Season 2019–20](/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Montenegrin_Second_League "2019–20 Montenegrin Second League") was interrupted after 30 weeks, due to the [coronavirus pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Montenegro "COVID-19 pandemic in Montenegro").[[2]](#cite_note-2) Therefore, [Dečić](/wiki/FK_De%C4%8Di%C4%87 "FK Dečić"), who had 10 points more than second-placed [Jezero](/wiki/FK_Jezero "FK Jezero"), gained direct promotion to Prva CFL. As Football Association of Montenegro decided, runner-up and third-placed squad at the moment of disruption (Jezero and [Bokelj](/wiki/FK_Bokelj "FK Bokelj")), participated in the playoffs for Prva CFL. While FK Jezero gained promotion to Prva CFL, FK Bokelj was eliminated after the penalties against [OFK Titograd](/wiki/OFK_Titograd "OFK Titograd").[[3]](#cite_note-3) From the other side, two worst-placed teams ([Lovćen](/wiki/FK_Lov%C4%87en "FK Lovćen") and [Otrant](/wiki/FK_Otrant "FK Otrant")) were relegated. That was the first time in the history when FK Lovćen, the oldest Montenegrin club, went to the bottom-tier. Except that, team from [Cetinje](/wiki/Cetinje "Cetinje") was relegated to [Montenegrin Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League") only one year after they played in [Prva CFL](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League") and in the final game of [Montenegrin Cup](/wiki/Montenegrin_Cup "Montenegrin Cup").  
[Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") won the title on [season 2020–21](/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_Montenegrin_Second_League "2020–21 Montenegrin Second League") and secured comeback to top-tier after two consecutive seasons in Second League. Second and third placed [Arsenal](/wiki/FK_Arsenal "FK Arsenal") and [Igalo](/wiki/OFK_Igalo "OFK Igalo") didn't succeed to gain promotion via playoffs, as they were defeated against [Iskra](/wiki/FK_Iskra_Danilovgrad "FK Iskra Danilovgrad") and [OFK Petrovac](/wiki/OFK_Petrovac "OFK Petrovac"). Two last-placed teams – [Ibar](/wiki/FK_Ibar "FK Ibar") and [Drezga](/wiki/FK_Drezga "FK Drezga") were relegated to Third League, both after two consecutive seasons spent in second-tier. During the season, Mornar made one of the all-time biggest victories in the history of competition, against Drezga (10–0).

### Relegation and promotion

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Relegation and promotion")]

See also: [Montenegrin First League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs") and [Montenegrin Third League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League#Promotion_playoffs "Montenegrin Third League")

At the end of every season, champion of Second League is directly promoted to [First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"), while last placed member of First League is moving to second-tier competition. Except that, second and third placed teams from Second League are participating in [First League playoffs](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League_playoffs "Montenegrin First League playoffs"). Their opponents are 8th and 9th team from the First League.  
From the other side, two last placed teams are directly relegated to [Montenegrin Third League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Third_League "Montenegrin Third League"). At the end of the season, winners of three Third League groups are participating in playoffs for Second League promotion. Two best placed teams from playoffs are gaining promotion to Montenegrin Second League.

### Changes in league structure

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Changes in league structure")]

In period 2006–2018, Montenegrin Second League consisted of 12 participants. From 2018 to 2019 season, the number of participants is reduced to 10, with 36 week-long competition.

* Number of teams:
  + 2006–07 to 2007–18: **12**
  + Since 2018–19: **10**

Logo and broadcasting
---------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Logo and broadcasting")]

### Official logo and equipment

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Official logo and equipment")]

Logo of Montenegrin Second League was presented in 2018, together with the new logos of [Montenegrin First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"), [Montenegrin Cup](/wiki/Montenegrin_Cup "Montenegrin Cup") and youth leagues.[[6]](#cite_note-6)  
Official ball of competition is produced under the [Derbystar](/w/index.php?title=Derbystar&action=edit&redlink=1 "Derbystar (page does not exist)") brand, while the official equipment of referees is product of [Legea](/wiki/Legea "Legea").

### Broadcasting rights

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Montenegrin_Second_League&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Broadcasting rights")]

Since foundation of the competition, official broadcaster of Second Montenegrin League matches is national television of Montenegro – [RTCG](/wiki/Radio_and_Television_of_Montenegro "Radio and Television of Montenegro").   
From season 2018–19, broadcaster of matches is cable-network channel [MNE Sport TV](/w/index.php?title=MNE_Sport_TV&action=edit&redlink=1 "MNE Sport TV (page does not exist)"). Every weekend, one game is broadcast on their channels.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

**Association football**, more commonly known as **football** or in some countries as **soccer**,[[a]](#cite_note-4) is a [team sport](/wiki/Team_sport "Team sport") played between two teams of 11 [players](/wiki/Football_player "Football player") who almost exclusively use their feet to propel a [ball](/wiki/Ball_(association_football) "Ball (association football)") around a [pitch](/wiki/Football_pitch "Football pitch").

The objective of the game is to [score](/wiki/Scoring_in_association_football "Scoring in association football") more goals than the opposing team by moving the ball beyond the goal line into a rectangular-framed [goal](/wiki/Goal_(sport) "Goal (sport)") defended by the opponent. Traditionally, the game has been played over two 45-minute halves, for a total match time of 90 minutes. With an estimated 250 million players active in over 200 countries and territories, it is the world's most popular sport.

Association football is played in accordance with the [Laws of the Game](/wiki/Laws_of_the_Game_(association_football) "Laws of the Game (association football)"), a set of rules that has been in effect since 1863 and maintained by the [IFAB](/wiki/International_Football_Association_Board "International Football Association Board") since 1886. The game is played with a football that is 68–70 cm (27–28 in) in [circumference](/wiki/Circumference "Circumference"). When the ball is in play, the players mainly use their feet, but may also use any other part of their body, except for their hands or arms, to control, strike, or pass the ball; the head, chest, and thighs are commonly used. Only the [goalkeepers](/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)") may use their hands and arms, but only within their own [penalty area](/wiki/Penalty_area "Penalty area"). Depending on the format of the competition, an equal number of goals scored may result in a [draw](/wiki/Tie_(draw)#Association_football "Tie (draw)") being declared with 1 point awarded to each team, or the game may go into [extra time](/wiki/Overtime_(sports)#Association_football "Overtime (sports)") or a [penalty shoot-out](/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)").[[4]](#cite_note-laws51-52-5)

Internationally, association football is governed by [FIFA](/wiki/FIFA "FIFA"). Under FIFA, there are six continental confederations: [AFC](/wiki/Asian_Football_Confederation "Asian Football Confederation"), [CAF](/wiki/Confederation_of_African_Football "Confederation of African Football"), [CONCACAF](/wiki/CONCACAF "CONCACAF"), [CONMEBOL](/wiki/CONMEBOL "CONMEBOL"), [OFC](/wiki/Oceania_Football_Confederation "Oceania Football Confederation"), and [UEFA](/wiki/UEFA "UEFA"). National associations (e.g. [the FA](/wiki/The_Football_Association "The Football Association") in England, [U.S. Soccer](/wiki/U.S._Soccer "U.S. Soccer") in the United States, etc.) are responsible for managing the game in their own countries both professionally and at an amateur level, and coordinating competitions in accordance with the Laws of the Game. The most prestigious senior international competition is the [FIFA World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup"). The men's World Cup is the most-viewed sporting event in the world, surpassing the [Olympic Games](/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games").[[5]](#cite_note-6) The most prestigious competition in European club football is the [UEFA Champions League](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League"), which attracts an extensive television audience worldwide. The final of the men's Champions League is the most-watched annual sporting event in the world.[[6]](#cite_note-7)[[7]](#cite_note-8)
