**Football** is a family of [team sports](/wiki/Team_sport "Team sport") in which the object is to get the [ball](/wiki/Football_(ball) "Football (ball)") over a goal line, into a goal, or between goalposts using merely the body (by carrying, throwing, or [kicking](/wiki/Kick_(football) "Kick (football)")).[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Unqualified, [the word *football*](/wiki/Football_(word) "Football (word)") generally means the form of football that is the most popular where the word is used. Sports commonly called *football* include [association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") (known as *soccer* in Australia, Canada, South Africa, the United States, and sometimes in Ireland and New Zealand); [Australian rules football](/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football"); [Gaelic football](/wiki/Gaelic_football "Gaelic football"); [gridiron football](/wiki/Gridiron_football "Gridiron football") (specifically [American football](/wiki/American_football "American football"), [arena football](/wiki/Arena_football "Arena football"), or [Canadian football](/wiki/Canadian_football "Canadian football")); [International rules football](/wiki/International_rules_football "International rules football"); [rugby league football](/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"); and [rugby union football](/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union").[[4]](#cite_note-4) These various forms of football share, to varying degrees, common origins and are known as "**football codes**".

There are a number of references to traditional, ancient, or prehistoric ball games played in many different parts of the world.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-fifa-or-7) Contemporary codes of football can be traced back to the codification of [these games at English public schools](/wiki/English_public_school_football_games "English public school football games") during the 19th century, itself an outgrowth of [medieval football](/wiki/Medieval_football "Medieval football").[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) The expansion and cultural power of the [British Empire](/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") allowed these rules of football to spread to areas of [British](/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") influence outside the directly controlled empire.[[10]](#cite_note-10) By the end of the 19th century, distinct regional codes were already developing: [Gaelic football](/wiki/Gaelic_football "Gaelic football"), for example, deliberately incorporated the rules of local traditional football games to maintain their heritage.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In 1888, the [Football League](/wiki/English_Football_League "English Football League") was founded in England, becoming the first of many professional football associations. During the 20th century, several of the various kinds of football grew to become some of the most popular [team sports](/wiki/Team_sport "Team sport") in the world.[[12]](#cite_note-Bale-12)

Common elements
---------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Lionel_Messi_Player_of_the_Year_2011.jpg/120px-Lionel_Messi_Player_of_the_Year_2011.jpg)](/wiki/File:Lionel_Messi_Player_of_the_Year_2011.jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Quinn_Nordin_%2830817577425%29.jpg/250px-Quinn_Nordin_%2830817577425%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Quinn_Nordin_(30817577425).jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Dana_Hooker_kicking.jpg/120px-Dana_Hooker_kicking.jpg)](/wiki/File:Dana_Hooker_kicking.jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/ST_vs_LOU_espoirs_2013_%2872%29.JPG/250px-ST_vs_LOU_espoirs_2013_%2872%29.JPG)](/wiki/File:ST_vs_LOU_espoirs_2013_(72).JPG)

The action of kicking in (clockwise from upper left) association, gridiron, rugby, and Australian football

The various codes of football share certain common elements and can be grouped into two main classes of football: *carrying* codes like American football, Canadian football, Australian football, rugby union and rugby league, where the ball is moved about the field while being held in the hands or passed by hand, and *kicking* codes such as association football and Gaelic football, where the ball is moved primarily with the feet, and where handling is strictly limited.[[13]](#cite_note-Douge-13)
Common rules among the sports include:[[14]](#cite_note-14)

* Two *teams* usually have between 11 and 18 players; some variations that have fewer players (five or more per team) are also popular.[[15]](#cite_note-15)
* A clearly defined area in which to play the game.
* *[Scoring](/wiki/Score_(sport) "Score (sport)")* *[goals](/wiki/Goal_(sport) "Goal (sport)")* or *points* by moving the ball to an opposing team's end of the field and either into a goal area, or over a line.
* Goals or points resulting from players putting the ball between two *[goalposts](/wiki/Goalposts "Goalposts")*.
* The goal or line being *defended* by the opposing team.
* Players using only their body to move the ball, i.e. no additional equipment such as bats or sticks.
* An inflatable [ball](/wiki/Football_(ball) "Football (ball)").

In all codes, common skills include [passing](/wiki/Passing_(sports) "Passing (sports)"), [tackling](/wiki/Tackle_(football_move) "Tackle (football move)"), evasion of tackles, catching and [kicking](/wiki/Kick_(football) "Kick (football)").[[13]](#cite_note-Douge-13) In most codes, there are rules restricting the movement of players *[offside](/wiki/Offside_(sport) "Offside (sport)")*, and players scoring a goal must put the ball either under or over a *[crossbar](/wiki/Goal_(sport) "Goal (sport)")* between the [goalposts](/wiki/Goal_(sports) "Goal (sports)").

Etymology
---------

Main article: [*Football* (word)](/wiki/Football_(word) "Football (word)")

There are conflicting explanations of the origin of the word "football". It is widely assumed that the word "football" (or the phrase "foot ball") refers to the action of the foot kicking a ball.[[16]](#cite_note-16) There is an alternative explanation, which is that football originally referred to a variety of games in [medieval Europe](/wiki/Medieval_Europe "Medieval Europe") that were played *on foot*.[[17]](#cite_note-17) There is little conclusive evidence for either explanation.

Early history
-------------

### Ancient games

See also: [Episkyros](/wiki/Episkyros "Episkyros") and [Cuju](/wiki/Cuju "Cuju")

#### Ancient China

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Emperor_Taizu_play_Cuju.jpg/250px-Emperor_Taizu_play_Cuju.jpg)](/wiki/File:Emperor_Taizu_play_Cuju.jpg)

[Emperor Taizu of Song](/wiki/Emperor_Taizu_of_Song "Emperor Taizu of Song") playing *[cuju](/wiki/Cuju "Cuju")* (Chinese football) with his prime minister [Zhao Pu](/wiki/Zhao_Pu "Zhao Pu") (趙普) and other ministers, by [Yuan dynasty](/wiki/Yuan_dynasty "Yuan dynasty") artist [Qian Xuan](/wiki/Qian_Xuan "Qian Xuan") (1235–1305)

The Chinese competitive game *[cuju](/wiki/Cuju "Cuju")* is an early type of ball game where feet were used, in some aspects resembling modern [association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football"). It was possibly played around the [Han dynasty](/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") and early [Qin dynasty](/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty"), based on an attestation in a military manual from around the second to third centuries BC.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20) In one version, gameplay consisted of players passing the ball between teammates without allowing it to touch the ground (much like [keepie uppie](/wiki/Keepie_uppie "Keepie uppie")).
In its competitive version, two teams had to pass the ball without it falling, before kicking the ball through a circular hole placed in the middle of the pitch. Unlike association football, the two teams did not interact with each other but instead stayed on opposite sides of the pitch.[[21]](#cite_note-21) Cuju has been cited by FIFA as the earliest form of football.[[7]](#cite_note-fifa-or-7)
The Japanese version of *cuju* is *[kemari](/wiki/Kemari "Kemari")* (蹴鞠), and was developed during the [Asuka period](/wiki/Asuka_period "Asuka period").[[22]](#cite_note-hawaii-22) This is known to have been played within the Japanese imperial court in [Kyoto](/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto") from about 600 AD. In *kemari*, several people stand in a circle and kick a ball to each other, trying not to let the ball drop to the ground.
The [Silk Road](/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road") facilitated the transmission of *cuju*, especially the game popular in the [Tang dynasty](/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty"), the period when the [inflatable](/wiki/Inflatable "Inflatable") ball was invented and replaced the stuffed ball.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

#### Ancient Greece and Rome

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Tombstone_of_Gaius_Laberius_with_harpastum_ball_in_Sinj%2C_Croatia.jpg/250px-Tombstone_of_Gaius_Laberius_with_harpastum_ball_in_Sinj%2C_Croatia.jpg)](/wiki/File:Tombstone_of_Gaius_Laberius_with_harpastum_ball_in_Sinj,_Croatia.jpg)

An [ancient Roman](/wiki/Ancient_Roman "Ancient Roman") tombstone of a boy with a [Harpastum](/wiki/Harpastum "Harpastum") ball from [Tilurium](/wiki/Tilurium "Tilurium") (modern [Sinj](/wiki/Sinj "Sinj"), Croatia)

The [Ancient Greeks](/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") and [Romans](/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") are known to have played many ball games, some of which involved the use of the feet. The [Roman](/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") game *[harpastum](/wiki/Harpastum "Harpastum")* is believed to have been adapted from a [Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") team game known as ἐπίσκυρος (*[episkyros](/wiki/Episkyros "Episkyros")*)[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25) or φαινίνδα (*phaininda*),[[26]](#cite_note-26) which is mentioned by a Greek playwright, [Antiphanes](/wiki/Antiphanes_of_Berge "Antiphanes of Berge") (388–311 BC) and later referred to by the Christian theologian [Clement of Alexandria](/wiki/Clement_of_Alexandria "Clement of Alexandria") (c. 150 – c. 215 AD). These games appear to have resembled [rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football").[[27]](#cite_note-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29)[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31) The Roman politician [Cicero](/wiki/Cicero "Cicero") (106–43 BC) describes the case of a man who was killed whilst having a shave when a ball was kicked into a barber's shop. Roman ball games already knew the air-filled ball, the *[follis](/wiki/Follis_(ball) "Follis (ball)")*.[[32]](#cite_note-32)[[33]](#cite_note-33) *Episkyros* is described as an early form of football by FIFA.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

#### Native Americans

There are a number of references to traditional, [ancient](/wiki/Ancient "Ancient"), or [prehistoric](/wiki/Prehistoric "Prehistoric") ball games, played by [indigenous peoples](/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") in many different parts of the world. For example, in 1586, men from a ship commanded by an English explorer named [John Davis](/wiki/John_Davis_(English_explorer) "John Davis (English explorer)") went ashore to play a form of football with [Inuit](/wiki/Inuit "Inuit") in Greenland.[[35]](#cite_note-35) There are later accounts of an Inuit game played on ice, called *Aqsaqtuk*. Each match began with two teams facing each other in parallel lines, before attempting to kick the ball through each other team's line and then at a goal. In 1610, [William Strachey](/wiki/William_Strachey "William Strachey"), a colonist at [Jamestown, Virginia](/wiki/Jamestown,_Virginia "Jamestown, Virginia") recorded a game played by Native Americans, called *Pahsaheman*.[[36]](#cite_note-36) *[Pasuckuakohowog](/wiki/Pasuckuakohowog "Pasuckuakohowog")*, a game similar to modern-day [association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") played amongst [Amerindians](/wiki/Amerindians "Amerindians"), was also reported as early as the 17th century.[[37]](#cite_note-37)
[Games played in Mesoamerica](/wiki/Mesoamerican_ballgame "Mesoamerican ballgame") with rubber balls by [indigenous peoples](/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") are also well-documented as existing since before this time,[[38]](#cite_note-38) but these had more similarities to basketball or volleyball, and no links have been found between such games and modern football sports. Northeastern American Indians, especially the [Iroquois](/wiki/Iroquois "Iroquois") Confederation, played a game which made use of net racquets to throw and catch a small ball; however, although it is a ball-goal foot game, [lacrosse](/wiki/Lacrosse "Lacrosse") (as its modern descendant is called) is likewise not usually classed as a form of "football".[[39]](#cite_note-39)

#### Oceania

On the [Australian continent](/wiki/Australian_continent "Australian continent") several tribes of [indigenous people](/wiki/Indigenous_Australians "Indigenous Australians") played kicking and catching games with stuffed balls which have been generalised by historians as *[Marn Grook](/wiki/Marn_Grook "Marn Grook")* ([Djab Wurrung](/wiki/Djab_Wurrung "Djab Wurrung") for "game ball"). The earliest historical account is an [anecdote](/wiki/Anecdote "Anecdote") from the 1878 book by [Robert Brough-Smyth](/wiki/Robert_Brough-Smyth "Robert Brough-Smyth"), *The Aborigines of Victoria*, in which a man called Richard Thomas is quoted as saying, in about 1841 in [Victoria, Australia](/wiki/Victoria,_Australia "Victoria, Australia"), that he had witnessed Aboriginal people playing the game: "Mr Thomas describes how the foremost player will drop kick a ball made from the skin of a [possum](/wiki/Phalangeriformes "Phalangeriformes") and how other players leap into the air to catch it." Some historians have theorised that *Marn Grook* was one of the [origins of](/wiki/Origins_of_Australian_football "Origins of Australian football") [Australian rules football](/wiki/Australian_rules_football "Australian rules football").
The [Māori](/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people "Māori people") in New Zealand played a game called [Kī-o-rahi](/wiki/K%C4%AB-o-rahi "Kī-o-rahi") consisting of teams of seven players play on a circular field divided into zones, and score points by touching the 'pou' (boundary markers) and hitting a central 'tupu' or target.[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41)
These games and others may well go far back into antiquity. However, the main sources of modern football codes appear to lie in western Europe, especially England.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

#### Turkic peoples

[Mahmud al-Kashgari](/wiki/Mahmud_al-Kashgari "Mahmud al-Kashgari") in his *[Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk](/wiki/D%C4%ABw%C4%81n_Lugh%C4%81t_al-Turk "Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk")*, described a game called *tepuk* among [Turks](/wiki/Turkic_peoples "Turkic peoples") in Central Asia. In the game, people try to attack each other's castle by kicking a ball made of sheep leather.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

### Medieval and early modern Europe

Further information: [Medieval football](/wiki/Medieval_football "Medieval football")

The [Middle Ages](/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") saw a huge rise in popularity of annual [Shrovetide football](/wiki/Shrovetide_football "Shrovetide football") matches throughout Europe, particularly in England. An early reference to a ball game played in [Britain](/wiki/England "England") comes from the 9th-century *[Historia Brittonum](/wiki/Historia_Brittonum "Historia Brittonum")*, attributed to [Nennius](/wiki/Nennius "Nennius"), which describes "a party of boys ... playing at ball".[[44]](#cite_note-44) References to a ball game played in northern France known as *[La Soule](/wiki/La_Soule "La Soule")* or *Choule*, in which the ball was propelled by hands, feet, and sticks,[[45]](#cite_note-45) date from the 12th century.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Mobfooty.jpg/250px-Mobfooty.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mobfooty.jpg)

An illustration of so-called "mob football"

The early forms of football played in England, sometimes referred to as "[mob football](/wiki/Medieval_football "Medieval football")", would be played in towns or between neighbouring villages, involving an unlimited number of players on opposing teams who would clash *en masse*,[[47]](#cite_note-47) struggling to move an item, such as inflated animal's [bladder](/wiki/Bladder "Bladder")[[48]](#cite_note-sportmatters-48) to particular geographical points, such as their opponents' church, with play taking place in the open space between neighbouring parishes.[[49]](#cite_note-49) The game was played primarily during significant religious festivals, such as Shrovetide, Christmas, or Easter,[[48]](#cite_note-sportmatters-48) and Shrovetide games have survived into the modern era in a number of English towns (see below).
The first detailed description of what was almost certainly football in England was given by [William FitzStephen](/wiki/William_FitzStephen "William FitzStephen") in about 1174–1183. He described the activities of London youths during the annual festival of [Shrove Tuesday](/wiki/Shrove_Tuesday "Shrove Tuesday"):

> After lunch all the youth of the city go out into the fields to take part in a ball game. The students of each school have their own ball; the workers from each city craft are also carrying their balls. Older citizens, fathers, and wealthy citizens come on horseback to watch their juniors competing, and to relive their own youth vicariously: you can see their inner passions aroused as they watch the action and get caught up in the fun being had by the carefree adolescents.[[50]](#cite_note-50)

Most of the very early references to the game speak simply of "ball play" or "playing at ball". This reinforces the idea that the games played at the time did not necessarily involve a ball being kicked.
An early reference to a ball game that was probably football comes from 1280 at [Ulgham](/wiki/Ulgham "Ulgham"), Northumberland, England: "Henry... while playing at ball.. ran against David".[[51]](#cite_note-Magoun-51) Football was played in Ireland in 1308, with a documented reference to John McCrocan, a spectator at a "football game" at [Newcastle, County Down](/wiki/Newcastle,_County_Down "Newcastle, County Down") being charged with accidentally stabbing a player named William Bernard.[[52]](#cite_note-52) Another reference to a football game comes in 1321 at [Shouldham](/wiki/Shouldham "Shouldham"), Norfolk, England: "[d]uring the game at ball as he kicked the ball, a lay friend of his... ran against him and wounded himself".[[51]](#cite_note-Magoun-51)
In 1314, [Nicholas de Farndone](/wiki/Nicholas_de_Farndone "Nicholas de Farndone"), [Lord Mayor of the City of London](/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_the_City_of_London "Lord Mayor of the City of London") issued a decree banning football in the French used by the English upper classes at the time. A translation reads: "[f]orasmuch as there is great noise in the city caused by hustling over large foot balls [*rageries de grosses pelotes de pee*][[53]](#cite_note-53) in the fields of the public from which many evils might arise which God forbid: we command and forbid on behalf of the king, on pain of imprisonment, such game to be used in the city in the future." This is the earliest reference to football.
In 1363, King [Edward III of England](/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") issued a proclamation banning "...handball, football, or hockey; coursing and cock-fighting, or other such idle games",[[54]](#cite_note-54) showing that "football" – whatever its exact form in this case – was being differentiated from games involving other parts of the body, such as handball.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Football_gravure_1750.jpg/250px-Football_gravure_1750.jpg)](/wiki/File:Football_gravure_1750.jpg)

"Football" in France, circa 1750

A game known as "football" was played in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") as early as the 15th century: it was prohibited by the [Football Act 1424](/wiki/Football_Act_1424 "Football Act 1424") and although the law fell into disuse it was not repealed until 1906. There is evidence for schoolboys playing a "football" ball game in [Aberdeen](/wiki/Aberdeen "Aberdeen") in 1633 (some references cite 1636) which is notable as an early allusion to what some have considered to be passing the ball. The word "pass" in the most recent translation is derived from "huc percute" (strike it here) and later "repercute pilam" (strike the ball again) in the original Latin. It is not certain that the ball was being struck between members of the same team. The original word translated as "goal" is "metum", literally meaning the "pillar at each end of the circus course" in a Roman chariot race. There is a reference to "get hold of the ball before [another player] does" (Praeripe illi pilam si possis agere) suggesting that handling of the ball was allowed. One sentence states in the original 1930 translation "Throw yourself against him" (Age, objice te illi).
King [Henry IV of England](/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England") also presented one of the earliest documented uses of the English word "football", in 1409, when he issued a proclamation forbidding the levying of money for "foteball".[[51]](#cite_note-Magoun-51)[[55]](#cite_note-Etymology-55)
There is also an account in [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") from the end of the 15th century of football being played at [Caunton](/wiki/Caunton "Caunton"), Nottinghamshire. This is the first description of a "kicking game" and the first description of [dribbling](/wiki/Dribbling "Dribbling"): "[t]he game at which they had met for common recreation is called by some the foot-ball game. It is one in which young men, in country sport, propel a huge ball not by throwing it into the air but by striking it and rolling it along the ground, and that not with their hands but with their feet... kicking in opposite directions." The chronicler gives the earliest reference to a football pitch, stating that: "[t]he boundaries have been marked and the game had started.[[51]](#cite_note-Magoun-51)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/The_Doonies_versus_the_Croonies_on_New_Year%E2%80%99s_Day%2C_by_Alexander_Carse.jpg/250px-The_Doonies_versus_the_Croonies_on_New_Year%E2%80%99s_Day%2C_by_Alexander_Carse.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_Doonies_versus_the_Croonies_on_New_Year%E2%80%99s_Day,_by_Alexander_Carse.jpg)

Oldest known painting of foot-ball in Scotland, by [Alexander Carse](/wiki/Alexander_Carse "Alexander Carse"), c. 1810

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/The_foot-ball_play_by_Alexander_Carse_maybe_1830.jpg/250px-The_foot-ball_play_by_Alexander_Carse_maybe_1830.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_foot-ball_play_by_Alexander_Carse_maybe_1830.jpg)

"Football" in Scotland, c. 1830

Other firsts in the medieval and [early modern](/wiki/Early_modern_Europe "Early modern Europe") eras:

* "A football", in the sense of a ball rather than a game, was first mentioned in 1486.[[55]](#cite_note-Etymology-55) This reference is in Dame [Juliana Berners](/wiki/Juliana_Berners "Juliana Berners")' *Book of [St Albans](/wiki/St_Albans "St Albans")*. It states: "a certain rounde instrument to play with ...it is an instrument for the foote and then it is calde in Latyn 'pila pedalis', a fotebal".[[51]](#cite_note-Magoun-51)
* A pair of football boots were ordered by King [Henry VIII of England](/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England "Henry VIII of England") in 1526.[[56]](#cite_note-56)
* Women playing a form of football was first described in 1580 by Sir [Philip Sidney](/wiki/Philip_Sidney "Philip Sidney") in one of his poems: "[a] tyme there is for all, my mother often sayes, when she, with skirts tuckt very hy, with girles at football playes".[[57]](#cite_note-57)
* The first references to *goals* are in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. In 1584 and 1602 respectively, [John Norden](/wiki/John_Norden "John Norden") and [Richard Carew](/wiki/Richard_Carew_(antiquary) "Richard Carew (antiquary)") referred to "goals" in [Cornish hurling](/wiki/Cornish_hurling "Cornish hurling"). Carew described how goals were made: "they pitch two bushes in the ground, some eight or ten foote asunder; and directly against them, ten or twelue [twelve] score off, other twayne in like distance, which they terme their Goales".[[58]](#cite_note-58) He is also the first to describe goalkeepers and passing of the ball between players.
* The first direct reference to *scoring a goal* is in [John Day](/wiki/John_Day_(dramatist) "John Day (dramatist)")'s play *The Blind Beggar of Bethnal Green* (performed circa 1600; published 1659): "I'll play a gole at [camp-ball](/wiki/Camping_(game) "Camping (game)")" (an extremely violent variety of football, which was popular in [East Anglia](/wiki/East_Anglia "East Anglia")). Similarly in a poem in 1613, [Michael Drayton](/wiki/Michael_Drayton "Michael Drayton") refers to "when the Ball to throw, and drive it to the Gole, in squadrons forth they goe".

### Calcio Fiorentino

Main article: [Calcio Fiorentino](/wiki/Calcio_Fiorentino "Calcio Fiorentino")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Calcio_fiorentino_1688.jpg/250px-Calcio_fiorentino_1688.jpg)](/wiki/File:Calcio_fiorentino_1688.jpg)

An illustration of the *Calcio Fiorentino* field and starting positions, from a 1688 book by Pietro di Lorenzo Bini

In the 16th century, the city of [Florence](/wiki/Florence "Florence") celebrated the period between [Epiphany](/wiki/Epiphany_(feast) "Epiphany (feast)") and [Lent](/wiki/Lent "Lent") by playing a game which today is known as "*calcio storico*" ("historic kickball") in the [Piazza Santa Croce](/wiki/Piazza_Santa_Croce "Piazza Santa Croce").[[59]](#cite_note-59) The young aristocrats of the city would dress up in fine silk costumes and embroil themselves in a violent form of football. For example, *calcio* players could punch, shoulder charge, and kick opponents. Blows below the belt were allowed. The game is said to have originated as a military training exercise. In 1580, Count Giovanni de' Bardi di Vernio wrote *Discorso sopra 'l giuoco del Calcio Fiorentino*. This is sometimes said to be the earliest code of rules for any football game. The game was not played after January 1739 (until it was revived in May 1930).

### Official disapproval and attempts to ban football

Main article: [Attempts to ban football games](/wiki/Attempts_to_ban_football_games "Attempts to ban football games")

There have been many attempts to ban football, from the [Middle Ages](/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") through to the modern day. The first such law was passed in England in 1314; it was followed by more than 30 in England alone between 1314 and 1667.[[60]](#cite_note-Women_Football_and_Europe-60): 6 Women were [banned from playing](/wiki/Bans_of_women%27s_association_football "Bans of women's association football") at English and Scottish Football League grounds in 1921, a ban that was only lifted in the 1970s. Female footballers still face similar problems in some parts of the world.
[American football](/wiki/American_football "American football") also faced pressures to ban the sport. The game played in the 19th century resembled [mob football](/wiki/Mob_football "Mob football") that developed in medieval Europe, including a version popular on university campuses known as [old division football](/wiki/Old_division_football "Old division football"), and several municipalities banned its play in the mid-19th century.[[61]](#cite_note-PFRA1-61)[[62]](#cite_note-ODF-62) By the 20th century, the game had evolved to a more rugby style game. In 1905, there were calls to ban [American football](/wiki/American_football "American football") in the U.S. due to its violence; a meeting that year was hosted by American president [Theodore Roosevelt](/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") led to sweeping rules changes that caused the sport to diverge significantly from its rugby roots to become more like the sport as it is played today.[[63]](#cite_note-63)

### English public schools

Main article: [English public school football games](/wiki/English_public_school_football_games "English public school football games")

While football continued to be played in various forms throughout Britain, its [public schools](/wiki/Public_school_(England) "Public school (England)") (equivalent to private schools in other countries) are widely credited with four key achievements in the creation of modern football codes. First of all, the evidence suggests that they were important in taking football away from its "mob" form and turning it into an organised team sport. Second, many early descriptions of football and references to it were recorded by people who had studied at these schools. Third, it was teachers, students, and former students from these schools who first codified football games, to enable matches to be played between schools. Finally, it was at English public schools that the division between "kicking" and "running" (or "carrying") games first became clear.
The earliest evidence that games resembling football were being played at English public schools – mainly attended by boys from the upper, upper-middle and professional classes – comes from the *Vulgaria* by William Herman in 1519. Herman had been headmaster at [Eton](/wiki/Eton_College "Eton College") and [Winchester](/wiki/Winchester_College "Winchester College") colleges and his [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") textbook includes a translation exercise with the phrase "We wyll playe with a ball full of wynde".[[64]](#cite_note-64)
[Richard Mulcaster](/wiki/Richard_Mulcaster "Richard Mulcaster"), a student at Eton College in the early 16th century and later headmaster at other English schools, has been described as "the greatest sixteenth Century advocate of football".[[65]](#cite_note-65) Among his contributions are the earliest evidence of organised team football. Mulcaster's writings refer to teams ("sides" and "parties"), positions ("standings"), a referee ("judge over the parties") and a coach "(trayning maister)". Mulcaster's "footeball" had evolved from the disordered and violent forms of traditional football:

> [s]ome smaller number with such overlooking, sorted into sides and standings, not meeting with their bodies so boisterously to trie their strength: nor shouldring or shuffing one an other so barbarously ... may use footeball for as much good to the body, by the chiefe use of the legges.[[66]](#cite_note-66)

In 1633, [David Wedderburn](/wiki/David_Wedderburn_(writer) "David Wedderburn (writer)"), a teacher from [Aberdeen](/wiki/Aberdeen "Aberdeen"), mentioned elements of modern football games in a short Latin textbook called *Vocabula.* Wedderburn refers to what has been translated into modern English as "keeping goal" and makes an allusion to passing the ball ("strike it here"). There is a reference to "get hold of the ball", suggesting that some handling was allowed. It is clear that the tackles allowed included the charging and holding of opposing players ("drive that man back").[[67]](#cite_note-67)
A more detailed description of football is given in [Francis Willughby](/wiki/Francis_Willughby "Francis Willughby")'s *Book of Games*, written in about 1660.[[68]](#cite_note-68) Willughby, who had studied at [Bishop Vesey's Grammar School](/wiki/Bishop_Vesey%27s_Grammar_School "Bishop Vesey's Grammar School"), [Sutton Coldfield](/wiki/Sutton_Coldfield "Sutton Coldfield"), is the first to describe goals and a distinct playing field: "a close that has a gate at either end. The gates are called Goals." His book includes a diagram illustrating a football field. He also mentions tactics ("leaving some of their best players to guard the goal"); scoring ("they that can strike the ball through their opponents' goal first win") and the way teams were selected ("the players being equally divided according to their strength and nimbleness"). He is the first to describe a "law" of football: "they must not strike [an opponent's leg] higher than the ball".[[69]](#cite_note-69)[[70]](#cite_note-70)
English public schools were the first to codify football games. In particular, they devised the first *offside* rules, during the late 18th century.[[71]](#cite_note-Carosi-71) In the earliest manifestations of these rules, players were "off their side" if they simply stood between the ball and the goal which was their objective. Players were not allowed to pass the ball forward, either by foot or by hand. They could only dribble with their feet, or advance the ball in a *[scrum](/wiki/Scrum_(rugby) "Scrum (rugby)")* or similar *formation*. However, offside laws began to diverge and develop differently at each school, as is shown by the rules of football from Winchester, [Rugby](/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School"), [Harrow](/wiki/Harrow_School "Harrow School") and [Cheltenham](/wiki/Cheltenham_School "Cheltenham School"), during between 1810 and 1850.[[71]](#cite_note-Carosi-71) The first known codes – in the sense of a set of rules – were those of Eton in 1815[[72]](#cite_note-Richard_William_Cox_2002_243-72) and [Aldenham](/wiki/Aldenham_School "Aldenham School") in 1825.[[72]](#cite_note-Richard_William_Cox_2002_243-72))
During the early 19th century, most working-class people in Britain had to work six days a week, often for over twelve hours a day. They had neither the time nor the inclination to engage in sport for recreation and, at the time, many [children were part of the labour force](/wiki/Child_labour#Industrial_Revolution "Child labour"). [Feast day](/wiki/Feast_day "Feast day") football played on the streets was in decline. Public school boys, who enjoyed some freedom from work, became the inventors of organised football games with formal codes of rules.
Football was adopted by a number of public schools as a way of encouraging competitiveness and keeping youths fit. Each school drafted its own rules, which varied widely between different schools and were changed over time with each new intake of pupils. Two schools of thought developed regarding rules. Some schools favoured a game in which the ball could be carried (as at Rugby, [Marlborough](/wiki/Marlborough_College "Marlborough College") and Cheltenham), while others preferred a game where kicking and dribbling the ball was promoted (as at Eton, Harrow, [Westminster](/wiki/Westminster_School "Westminster School") and [Charterhouse](/wiki/Charterhouse_School "Charterhouse School")). The division into these two camps was partly the result of circumstances in which the games were played. For example, Charterhouse and Westminster at the time had restricted playing areas; the boys were confined to playing their ball game within the school [cloisters](/wiki/Cloisters "Cloisters"), making it difficult for them to adopt rough and tumble running games.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Rugby_School_850.jpg/250px-Rugby_School_850.jpg)](/wiki/File:Rugby_School_850.jpg)

Although the [Rugby School](/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School") (pictured) became famous due to a version that [rugby football](/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") was invented there in 1823, most sports historians refuse this version stating it is apocryphal.

[William Webb Ellis](/wiki/William_Webb_Ellis "William Webb Ellis"), a pupil at Rugby School, is said to have "with a fine disregard for the rules of football, *as played in his time* [emphasis added], first took the ball in his arms and ran with it, thus creating the distinctive feature of the rugby game." in 1823. This act is usually said to be the beginning of Rugby football, but there is little evidence that it occurred, and most sports historians believe the story to be apocryphal. The act of 'taking the ball in his arms' is often misinterpreted as 'picking the ball up' as it is widely believed that Webb Ellis' 'crime' was handling the ball, as in modern association football, however handling the ball at the time was often permitted and in some cases compulsory,[[73]](#cite_note-73) the rule for which Webb Ellis showed disregard was *running forward with it* as the rules of his time only allowed a player to retreat backwards or kick forwards.
[The boom in rail transport in Britain](/wiki/Railway_Mania "Railway Mania") during the 1840s meant that people were able to travel farther and with less inconvenience than they ever had before. Inter-school sporting competitions became possible. However, it was difficult for schools to play each other at football, as each school played by its own rules. The solution to this problem was usually that the match be divided into two-halves, one half played by the rules of the host "home" school, and the other half by the visiting "away" school.
The *modern* rules of many football codes were formulated during the mid- or late- 19th century. This also applies to other sports such as lawn bowls, lawn tennis, etc. The major impetus for this was the patenting of the world's first [lawnmower](/wiki/Lawnmower "Lawnmower") in 1830. This allowed for the preparation of modern ovals, playing fields, pitches, grass courts, etc.[[74]](#cite_note-74)
Apart from Rugby football, the public school codes have barely been played beyond the confines of each school's playing fields. However, many of them are still played at the schools which created them (see [§ British schools](#British_schools)).
In 1845, three boys at Rugby school were tasked with codifying the rules then being used at the school. These were the first set of written rules (or code) for any form of football.[[75]](#cite_note-75) This further assisted the spread of the Rugby game.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/The_Football_Game._Thomas_Webster%2C_1839%2C_1.jpg/500px-The_Football_Game._Thomas_Webster%2C_1839%2C_1.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_Football_Game._Thomas_Webster,_1839,_1.jpg)

*A Football Game* (1839) by British painter [Thomas Webster](/wiki/Thomas_Webster_(painter) "Thomas Webster (painter)")

Public schools' dominance of sports in the UK began to wane after the [Factory Act 1850](/wiki/Factory_Act_1850 "Factory Act 1850"), which significantly increased the recreation time available to working class children. Before 1850, many British children had to work six days a week, for more than twelve hours a day. From 1850, they could not work before 6 a.m. (7 a.m. in winter) or after 6 p.m. on weekdays (7 p.m. in winter); on Saturdays they had to cease work at 2 pm. These changes meant that working class children had more time for games, including various forms of football.
